Moreover, D-1 modulated extracellular polymeric substances, restraining their overproduction while enriching tyrosine- and tryptophan-like components to reinforce the interfacial barrier. Transcriptomic profiling further revealed downregulation of stress-defense genes (e.g., DNA repair and photoprotection) and restoration of growth-related pathways, including photosynthesis and energy metabolism. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish a community-to-strain paradigm for phycosphere microbiome-mediated tolerance of microalgae to NP, deepen our understanding of inter-species cooperation, and provide a basis for designing tailored algae-bacteria consortia for bioremediation.

title: Mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membranes facilitate gastric epithelial injury in hypoxia-induced gastric mucosal lesions
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hypoxia following mucosal congestion in clinical practice causes a wide range of gastrointestinal symptoms and induces profound structural and functional perturbations in mitochondria-associated ER membranes (MAMs), which are subcellular compartments whose integrity and stability are regulated by FUN14 domain-containing protein 1 (FUNDC1). OBJECTIVES: To investigate the effect of hypoxia-induced MAMs formation on gastric mucosal lesions in patients with severe hepatic disorders. METHODS: Liver cirrhosis (LC) and hepatic failure (HF) were selected as representative severe hepatic diseases, and gastric mucosal tissues were collected. We applied the gastrointestinal symptom rating scale (GSRS) and endoscopic images to evaluate the possible relationship between gastrointestinal symptoms and mucosal lesions. Portal hypertension (PHT)-induced mouse models and hypoxia-induced cell models were also established. The roles of FUNDC1, hypoxia-induced MAMs formation and mitochondrial oxidative stress in mucosal epithelial injury were analyzed. RESULTS: Patients with LC or HF frequently experienced gastrointestinal symptoms, which were correlated with the progression of gastric mucosal lesions. Hypoxia induced the upregulated expression of HIF-1α in gastric mucosal tissues, which was directly associated with the FUNDC1 promoter region, thereby increasing FUNDC1 gene transcription. Moreover, METTL3-mediated m6A methylation of FUNDC1 established a posttranscriptional regulatory layer to collectively drive upregulation of FUNDC1 expression. In addition, the increased level of FUNDC1 facilitated the formation of MAMs, drove a metabolic shift toward increased glycolysis, and elicited mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production. Ultimately, this increase in mtROS generation promoted NINJ1 oligomerization/activation to exacerbate gastric epithelial cell death and mucosal injury. CONCLUSION: Under hypoxic conditions, FUNDC1-regulated MAMs formation and mitochondrial oxidative stress play pivotal roles in the development of gastric mucosal lesions.

title: Corrigendum to “Global genomics of Lactococcus lactis: horizontal gene transfer and intergenic variation drive multiple domestication and dairy adaptation” [J. Adv. Res. 83 (2026) 25–36]
Corrigendum to “Nano-honokiol ameliorates the cognitive deficits in TgCRND8 mice of Alzheimer’s disease via inhibiting neuropathology and modulating gut microbiota” [J. Adv. Res. 35 (2021) 231–243]
abstract: honokiol ameliorates the cognitive deficits in TgCRND8 mice of Alzheimer's disease via inhibiting neuropathology and modulating gut microbiota"

title: Integrative multiomics and machine learning identify uridine as a candidate modulator of MMP7-mediated immune cell infiltration in pulmonary fibrosis
abstract: Introduction Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease (ILD) characterized by immune cell infiltration and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. Effective therapies remain limited. Uridine is an endogenous nucleoside with pro-reparative and immunomodulatory effects, but its molecular targets and immune mechanisms in IPF remain unclear. Objectives To identify potential uridine-associated targets in pulmonary fibrosis and to determine whether uridine is associated with matrix metalloproteinase 7 (MMP7)-related immune cell infiltration. Methods Uridine target predictions from multiple databases were integrated with bulk lung transcriptomes from three public ILD cohorts (n = 531). Machine learning with SHAP interpretation prioritized candidate targets. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) evaluated uridine-protein interactions. Single-cell RNA-seq (∼540,000 cells) and spatial transcriptomics (19 IPF, 6 controls) mapped the cellular and spatial distribution of MMP7 and linked MMP7-enriched compartments to immune infiltration signatures. Key findings were validated in a bleomycin (BLM)-induced mouse model and in vitro assays. Results Integrative analyses prioritized five core genes ( CA4 , MME , MMP7 , PTPRB , and TYMS ; individual AUCs > 0.85), with MMP7 showing the highest SHAP importance. Higher MMP7 expression was associated with worse survival (HR = 2.93, p < 0.001). Single-cell and spatial analyses showed MMP7 enrichment in secretory epithelial cells, and MMP7-positive spot proportions correlated with histologic fibrosis severity (r = 0.807, p = 2.93 × 10 −5 ). SPR confirmed direct uridine-MMP7 binding (KD = 6.73 × 10 −6 M). In the BLM model, uridine attenuated fibrotic pathology and immune cell infiltration (total CD45 + cells: 777.8 vs. 3745 in BLM, p = 0.0002), accompanied by changes in MMP7, MIF, and MDK, consistent with modulation of immune microenvironment features. Conclusion Integrative multiomics and machine learning analyses, together with in vitro and in vivo validation, suggest that uridine attenuates pulmonary fibrosis, potentially through modulation of MMP7-associated immune-microenvironment remodeling

title: Gravity-shaped plant architecture to enhance dense planting, lodging resistance and substance uptake and their applications in maize and other crop breeding
abstract: BACKGROUND: Gravity is a ubiquitous environmental force that shapes plant architecture. Shoots occupy aerial space to absorb light and carbon dioxide, while roots spread in soil to capture water and nutrients. To ensure plants obtain survival resources, gravity not only promotes vertical growth and thus resists lodging, but also enables plants to stretch horizontally with a certain lateral organ angle and thus affects their high-density planting tolerance. Meanwhile, a large root angle often enhances plant lodging resistance. Further, roots with flexible angles and depth can cope with complex soil conditions and ensure substance uptake. To date, a growing number of gravitropic genes have been identified in crops. However, most studies have focused on individual genes within specific regulation pathways, leading to a fragmented understanding of gravitropic regulation mechanisms. Therefore, a systematic summary of recent progress in this field is needed. AIM OF REVIEW: This review provides systematic insights into gravity-shaped plant architecture, which is critical to molecular breeding of maize and other crops to enhance dense planting, lodging resistance, and substance uptake. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS OF REVIEW: In this review, we systematically organized the molecular mechanisms of gravity signaling in plants and highlighted advances over the past few decades. Next, we analyzed gravitropic genes in crops that control agronomic traits to enhance crop dense planting, lodging resistance, and substance uptake, such as rice tiller angle, maize leaf angle, root growth angle and depth, and uptake of water, nutrients, and ions, and then predicted potential 69 gravitropic genes simultaneously related to these breeding traits in maize through homology alignment and expressing tissue analysis. Furthermore, the significance of gravitropic genes in maize and other crop breeding is explored. Finally, we discussed the importance of molecular gravitropism and outlined future research strategies on its breeding applications.

title: Micro- and nanoplastic exposure and human health
abstract: BACKGROUND: Microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs), collectively referred to as micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs), are pervasive environmental contaminants. In this review, MPs are defined as solid polymer-containing particles from 1 μm to 5 mm, whereas NPs range from 1 nm to < 1 μm. They originate from plastic degradation and the direct release of particles from industrial and consumer products. Human exposure occurs primarily through ingestion, inhalation, and dermal contact and may also occur through maternal-fetal transfer and medical materials. MNPs have been detected in human tissues and biological fluids, raising concerns about potential health effects; however, detection alone does not establish disease causation. AIM OF REVIEW: This review summarizes current knowledge on the sources, characteristics, exposure pathways, detection methods, and biological effects of MNPs. It critically integrates experimental, epidemiological, and analytical evidence to evaluate potential health risks and identify key knowledge gaps. Where evidence permits, MPs and NPs are discussed separately, and human observations are distinguished from in vitro and animal findings. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS OF REVIEW: Experimental evidence suggests that MNP exposure may affect multiple biological systems through oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic disturbance, and immune dysregulation. Adverse effects have been reported across multiple organ systems in experimental studies, whereas human epidemiological evidence remains limited and insufficient to establish causality. NPs may exhibit greater cellular uptake and biological-barrier translocation than larger MPs, depending on particle properties and biological context. Heterogeneity in particle characteristics, exposure scenarios, and analytical methods complicates cross-study comparisons and risk evaluation. Many mechanistic studies also use pristine model particles and exposure doses that may not reflect real-world conditions. Standardized detection and exposure assessment, environmentally relevant models, and well-designed human studies are therefore needed to clarify the long-term health implications of chronic low-dose MNP exposure and support future risk assessment.

title: Heat-inactivated probiotic-fermented tamarind pulp alleviates constipation by modulating gut tryptophan catabolism and the AhR NLRP3 axis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Constipation is a common gastrointestinal disorder with gut dysbiosis, and existing laxatives often have limitations, necessitating the development of safer and more effective nutritional interventions. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the alleviating effects and potential mechanisms of probiotic-fermented tamarind pulp (FTP) on loperamide-induced constipation in mice. METHODS: A constipated mouse model was established and treated with low and high-dose FTP (LD‑FTP and HD‑FTP). Assessments included gastrointestinal transit, histopathology, serum neurotransmitters/inflammatory factors, gut microbiota (16S rRNA amplicon sequencing), functional predictions generated using PICRUSt2, and fecal metabolomics (LC-MS). RESULTS: FTP dose-dependently alleviated loperamide‑induced constipation. Compared with the model group, HD‑FTP increased small intestinal transit rate by 57.2% (to 92.95%, p < 0.001) and fecal water content by 65.9% (to 70.52%, p < 0.001), both effects superior to the positive control bisacodyl. HD‑FTP also reduced serum IL‑6, IL‑1β, and TNF‑α by 60.0%, 43.5%, and 45.4%, respectively (all p < 0.001), and elevated total short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) by 107.4% (p < 0.001). FTP exhibited significantly superior constipation‑alleviating efficacy compared to unfermented tamarind pulp (UFTP). FTP also increased microbial richness, enriched potentially beneficial SCFA-producing taxa, and restored microbial metabolic pathways associated with SCFA biosynthesis. Notably, fermentation enhanced tryptophan metabolism toward indole and serotonin pathways, which correlated with increased aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) activation and reduced NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in the colon. CONCLUSION: FTP effectively alleviated constipation by improving intestinal function, reducing inflammation, and remodeling the gut microbiota-metabolite axis. Mechanistically, fermentation-driven tryptophan catabolism and quercetin biotransformation converge on the AhR-NLRP3 axis. These findings highlight FTP as a superior nutritional strategy over UFTP.

title: Aebp1 drives a ceramide-gated Calhm2 calcium influx that injures podocytes in diabetic kidney disease
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Podocyte injury is a critical determinant of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and other proteinuric nephropathies; however, the mechanisms linking lipotoxicity to cytoskeletal disruption remain unclear. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify a central regulator linking lipotoxicity to podocyte injury, decipher its downstream pathway to pathological calcium influx, and assess its translational potential as a non-invasive biomarker of disease progression. METHODS: Integrated transcriptomic-proteomic analysis of diabetic glomeruli identified Adipocyte Enhancer-Binding Protein 1 (Aebp1). Its function was investigated using renal overexpression and podocyte-specific knockout mouse models of diabetic and adriamycin (ADR) nephropathy. Mechanistic studies combined in vitro and in vivo analyses, including intracellular calcium kinetic assays and direct protein-lipid interaction assays (e.g., surface plasmon resonance). Clinical validation was conducted in a biopsy-proven DKD cohort, correlating urinary Aebp1 levels with histological severity and longitudinal estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline. RESULTS: Aebp1 was identified as a progressively upregulated gene in the diabetic glomeruli. In mice, renal overexpression of Aebp1 induced proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis, whereas podocyte-specific knockout conferred protection against injury in diabetic mice. Mechanistically, Aebp1 activated NF-κB signaling, leading to Neu3 upregulation and pathogenic ceramide accumulation in the podocytes. We found that ceramide can directly bind to and activate Calhm2, a calcium channel not previously implicated in kidney physiology, suggesting a novel lipid-gated pathway linking lipotoxicity to pathological calcium influx in podocytes. This mechanism has been validated in ADR-induced nephropathy. Clinically, urinary Aebp1 serves as an independent predictor of histologically confirmed glomerulosclerosis severity and predicts the clinical endpoint of ≥ 30% eGFR decline. CONCLUSION: This study identifies a potential pathway in which Aebp1 promotes ceramide accumulation which may activate the Calhm2 calcium channel, thus linking lipotoxicity to calcium dysregulation and podocyte injury in DKD and other proteinuric conditions. Urinary Aebp1 is a potential clinically non-invasive biomarker for predicting histological damage and functional decline in DKD.

title: A JAZ-VQ-WRKY transcriptional feedback loop enforces homeostasis in cytotoxic alkaloid biosynthesis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Plants face the challenge of balancing the production of defense-related secondary metabolites, requiring inducible "accelerators" and intrinsic "braking" systems to avoid overproduction. While the phytohormone jasmonate (JA) is a well-established accelerator, the molecular nature of the braking machinery and its coordination with JA signaling remain unclear. The medicinal plant Catharanthus roseus produces cytotoxic terpenoid indole alkaloids (TIAs) and serves as an ideal system to address this question. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to identify the core JA-induced transcription factors regulating TIAs synthesis, and to elucidate how their activity is precisely constrained to prevent metabolic runaway, thereby deciphering the molecular mechanisms by which plants achieve metabolic homeostasis. METHODS: We used DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq), yeast one-hybrid (Y1H), and dual luciferase reporter (Dual-LUC) assays to identify and validate the direct binding and transactivation of the transcription factor CrWRKY4 on TIAs pathway genes. Gene knockout was achieved in hairy roots using an optimized CRISPR/Cas9 system. Protein interactions were analyzed using yeast two-hybrid (Y2H), bimolecular complementation (BiFC), and immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) techniques. The functional role of the regulatory module was systematically elucidated through subcellular localization studies, electrophoresis mobility shift assay (EMSA), and metabolite quantification (UPLC-QQQ-MS/MS). RESULTS: We identified a JA-inducible master regulator transcription factor, CrWRKY4, it directly binds and activates multiple TIAs pathway genes. Concurrently, two co-repressors, CrVQ4 and CrVQ9, were characterized and inhibit CrWRKY4's DNA-binding capacity. Moreover, CrJAZ1 interacts with VQ proteins and interferes with the VQ-WRKY regulatory complex. Crucially, CrWRKY4 directly activates the expression of CrVQ4, CrVQ9, and CrJAZ1, forming an intrinsic negative feedback loop. Upon JA signaling, the repressive CrJAZ1-CrVQ4/9 module is relieved, allowing CrWRKY4 to activate TIAs gene expression. CONCLUSION: This study elucidates a core regulatory mechanism comprising the CrJAZ1-CrVQ4/9-CrWRKY4 module. This module forms a self-braking transcriptional circuit by integrating JA signal.

title: The oval bed nucleus of the stria terminalis endocannabinoid signaling constrains post-traumatic stress disorder-like behaviors
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) develops when acute threat responses fail to resolve, resulting in persistent anxiety, avoidance, and hyperarousal. However, the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms governing the transition from acute stress to enduring pathology remain incompletely understood. Objectives This study aimed to determine whether endocannabinoid (eCB) signaling within posterior basolateral amygdala (pBLA) to oval bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (ovBNST) projections constrains the maladaptive transition from social threat to PTSD-like anxiety and defensive states. METHODS: Using a modified 5-day chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) paradigm, we employed a multimodal experimental strategy that included in vivo fiber photometry, molecular analyses, optogenetic manipulation, pharmacological intervention, and genetic perturbation to interrogate neuronal activity and modulate eCB signaling dynamics in the ovBNST, followed by stress-related behavioral assays. Genetic suppression of 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) synthesis was employed to evaluate circuit-specific eCB function. RESULTS: Both acute social defeat and trauma re-experiencing enhanced ovBNST neuronal activity and eCB signaling. CSDS reduced pBLA Cnr1 mRNA expression and ovBNST cannabinoid type-1 receptor (CB1R) protein levels, leading to heightened ovBNST excitability, likely due to diminished presynaptic inhibition of glutamate release from pBLA-ovBNST terminals. Pharmacological inhibition of 2-AG degradation in the ovBNST or optogenetic activation of CB1Rs in pBLA-ovBNST projections reversed CSDS-induced social avoidance and anxiety-like behaviors. In contrast, genetic suppression of 2-AG synthesis exacerbated PTSD-like phenotypes. CONCLUSION: These findings identify a social threat-responsive pBLA-ovBNST circuit in which eCB signaling modulates glutamatergic transmission to promote resilience against PTSD-like behavioral states. Restoring eCB homeostasis within this pathway may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for PTSD intervention.

title: TERT is a therapeutic target for tertiary stroke prevention
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Tertiary stroke prevention aims to mitigate long-term disability and improve life quality for stroke survivors. While primary and secondary stroke prevention strategies have been extensively investigated, tertiary prevention remains a critically understudied area, and there is currently no clinically approved drug for tertiary stroke prevention. OBJECTIVES: We previously discovered a transcription-regulatory function of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) in cultured primary neurons. Here, we further explored the in vivo role of TERT in neural repair and functional recovery after ischemic stroke. METHODS: We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis in a photothrombosis (PT)-induced permanent ischemic stroke mouse model to characterize TERT expression in the cerebral peri-infarct tissue, which was verified by PT and middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mouse model with immunofluorescence analysis. CUT&Tag-sequencing was used to profile the whole-genome TERT binding loci and transcriptional activity in the isolated neurons from the peri-infarct tissue. We further used phospho-proteomic analysis to identify the signaling mechanism of TERT regulation in neurons. RESULTS: snRNA-seq revealed TERT expression was increased in neurons in the peri-infarct tissue during the critical post-stroke recovery period in PT mice. This result was confirmed by immunofluorescent imaging in the PT and MCAO stroke models. Intravenous delivery of brain-targeted AAV-mediated neuron-specific overexpression of TERT significantly bolstered neural repair and functional recovery in the PT stroke model. Additionally, pharmacological upregulation of TERT expression in post-stroke recovery period by oral gavage of cycloastragenol (CAG) conferred prominent neural repair, improved sensorimotor functional recovery and alleviated post-stroke depression-like behaviors. Knockdown of neuronal TERT abolished the spontaneous and CAG-induced neural repair-promoting effect in PT mice. Mechanistically, we discovered that neuronal TERT is a transcriptional co-regulator of CREB-target genes including GAP43, EVL, NR4A3, and NRP2 which are associated with enhanced axon sprouting, dendritic branching and synaptogenesis in recovery phase of PT stroke. We further demonstrated that CAG upregulates TERT expression by promoting STAT3 phosphorylation at serine 727 in a DAPK1-dependent manner. CONCLUSION: Overall, these results demonstrate that TERT is a promising therapeutic target for tertiary stroke prevention.

title: Sequential modulation of the cGAS-STING pathway promotes spinal cord injury repair
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The cGAS-STING pathway is a central innate immune sensor of cytosolic DNA. Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers sterile inflammation, but the spatiotemporal role of this pathway in injured spinal cord repair remains unclear. Understanding its phase-dependent functions may enable precise immunomodulation to improve recovery. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the dynamic activation of the cGAS-STING pathway after SCI and to determine whether a time-sequenced pharmacological strategy, consisting of early activation followed by late inhibition, could enhance functional repair. METHODS: A mouse thoracic compressive SCI model was used. Pathway expression and cellular localization were assessed by western blot, immunofluorescence, and transcriptomics. Sustained or sequential modulation was performed using STING agonists and antagonists. Motor recovery was evaluated by the Basso Mouse Scale and footprint analysis. Axonal integrity, myelin preservation, and glial scarring were analyzed histologically. Myeloid cells (including microglia) were depleted with PLX5622, and neuron-microglia cocultures were established for mechanistic studies. RESULTS: cGAS-STING was significantly activated predominantly in myeloid cells (mainly microglia, with a smaller contribution from infiltrating macrophages) after SCI. Sustained activation or inhibition failed to improve recovery. Sequential treatment (ADU-S100 days 0-10 → C-176 days 11-28) markedly enhanced motor function, axonal integrity, and myelin preservation while reducing glial scarring. Mechanistically, early activation boosted microglial phagocytosis and clearance; late inhibition resolved inflammation and promoted the expression of anti-inflammatory and axon-associated genes. Myeloid cell depletion completely abolished these benefits. CONCLUSION: The cGAS-STING pathway exerts phase‑dependent, biphasic functions in SCI. A precisely timed "activation followed by inhibition" strategy optimally harnesses myeloid cell dynamics to coordinate debris clearance and inflammation resolution, offering a novel immunomodulatory paradigm for central nervous system repair.

title: Multi-omics reveals a host-microbe metabolic synergy underlying brown planthopper biotype divergence
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The brown planthopper (BPH) is a highly destructive pest in rice production. The widespread cultivation of resistant rice varieties drives BPH populations to evolve new biotypes, posing a continuous challenge to crop protection. Understanding the adaptation mechanisms of these biotypes is therefore critical. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the potential mechanisms underlying the adaptation of a new BPH biotype to resistant rice varieties. METHODS: We compared the host adaptability of Biotype 1 and Biotype Y on a resistant rice variety (carring Bph15). An integrative multi-omics approach (transcriptomic and metabolomic) was employed, alongside metagenomic analysis of symbiotic microbiota. RESULTS: Biotype Y exhibited superior adaptation to the resistant variety. Multi-omics analysis revealed that the adaptation was associated with upregulation of carbohydrate, detoxification, and energy metabolism pathways, downregulation of vitamin pathways, and a distinct symbiotic microbiota enriched in Wolbachia. Functional experiments provided evidence suggesting that Wolbachia may contribute to this enhanced adaptation, possibly through riboflavin supplementation. CONCLUSION: The adaptation of BPH to resistant rice appears to be associated with coordinated transcriptional and metabolic reprogramming, potentially involving symbiont-mediated nutritional support. These findings may provide new insights into tripartite host-pest-microbiota interactions and offer potential targets for sustainable pest management strategies.

title: HFPO homologue exposure impairs human sperm function via calcium dyshomeostasis and mitochondrial dysfunction
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hexafluoropropylene oxide homologues (HFPOs), developed as alternatives to the banned perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), are environmentally persistent and increasingly detected. However, despite some evidence of reproductive toxicity, their direct impact on human sperm function has not been characterized. OBJECTIVES: This study investigated the reproductive toxicity of three prevalent HFPOs (hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid, HFPO-DA; hexafluoropropylene oxide trimer acid, HFPO-TA; and hexafluoropropylene oxide tetramer acid, HFPO-TeA) using an in vitro human spermatozoa exposure model, and further explored the underlying mechanisms. METHODS: In vitro assays were conducted using human spermatozoa to assess reproductive toxicity upon exposure to three prevalent HFPOs. Sperm motility, viability, and fertilization potential were assessed. Mitochondrial integrity and function, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, calcium homeostasis, and metabolic and proteomic profiles were evaluated. The CatSper channel blocker NNC 55-0396 was used to examine calcium influx. Progesterone-mediated acrosome reaction, sperm penetration capability, and calcium signaling were determined. The mitochondria-targeted antioxidant mitoquinone was applied to evaluate protection against HFPO-induced toxicity. RESULTS: HFPO exposure, particularly HFPO-TeA and HFPO-TA, significantly impaired mitochondrial integrity and function, elevated ROS generation, disrupted calcium homeostasis, and perturbed metabolic and proteomic profiles. These effects culminated in compromised sperm motility, viability, and fertilization potential. Notably, the CatSper channel blocker NNC 55-0396 markedly inhibited HFPO-induced calcium influx. Furthermore, HFPOs significantly suppressed progesterone-mediated acrosome reaction, as well as sperm penetration capability and calcium signaling. Conversely, the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant mitoquinone significantly attenuated HFPO-caused toxicity to human sperm. CONCLUSION: These findings identify HFPOs as reproductive toxicants that compromise male fertility through disruption of calcium signaling and mitochondrial function. Our results underscore the urgent need for risk assessment and regulatory measures to address these emerging contaminants.

title: S1R/5-HT1AR heterocomplex mediated disinhibition of the DRN5-HT-mPFCpyr circuit underlies the faster-onset antidepressant-like effect of sigma-1 receptor activation
abstract: Background The Sigma-1 receptor (S1R) represents a promising target for faster-onset antidepressants. Nevertheless, the mechanism underlying the delayed onset of therapeutic action exhibited by S1R-activating selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) remains unclear. Thus, elucidating the role of S1R in mediating faster antidepressant-like effects is of considerable significance. Objective This study aimed to elucidate the role of S1R in mediating faster onset antidepressant-like effects and to investigate the underlying mechanism. Methods To detect the formation of S1R/5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 1A (5-HT 1A R) heterocomplexes, in situ proximity ligation assay, co-immunoprecipitation, and co-localization techniques were employed. The functional role of these heterocomplexes was assessed through pharmacological interventions and behavioral tests. Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying their faster antidepressant-like effects were investigated using electrophysiological recordings and chemogenetic approaches. Results We provide evidence for the existence of S1R/5-HT 1A R heterocomplexes in the mouse brain through in-situ PLA and co-immunoprecipitation, and by co-localization assays in primary cortical neurons, and further reveal that these heterocomplexes are predominantly localized in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN). Pharmacological activation of S1R promoted 5‑HT 1A R trafficking to the plasma membrane and enhanced functional heterocomplex formation. CREB luciferase reporter assays revealed that S1R/5‑HT 1A R heterocomplexes suppress 8‑OH‑DPAT-induced inhibition of forskolin-induced CREB signaling in cells co‑expressing both receptors. Electrophysiological recordings indicated that the heterocomplex attenuated the ability of 5‑HT 1A R to open G protein‑gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels, thus preventing excessive neuronal hyperpolarization and promoting neuronal activity. Disrupting S1R/5‑HT 1A R complexes in DRN induced depressive‑like behaviors in mice, whereas specific activation of the DRN 5-HTergic to medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) pyramidal (DRN 5-HT -mPFC pyr ) neuronal circuit alleviated these behavioral deficits. Conclusion Our findings demonstrate that S1R/5-HT 1A R heterocomplex activity mediates disinhibition within the DRN 5-HT -mPFC pyr neuronal circuit, underpinning the rapid antidepressant-like effects elicited by S1R activation. This highlights S1R as a promising therapeutic target for the development of faster-onset antidepressants.

title: Hyodeoxycholic acid rejuvenates BMSCs against postmenopausal osteoporosis by attenuating senescence and aberrant adipogenesis via TGR5-ESR1-mediated mitophagy
abstract: Introduction Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMOP) is driven by bone marrow stromal cell (BMSC) senescence and aberrant adipogenesis, with 17β-estradiol (E2) deficiency as a primary trigger. However, the metabolic mediators linking systemic E2 loss to BMSC dysfunction remain undefined. Bile acids are established endogenous “metabolic rejuvenators,” but the functional relevance of hyodeoxycholic acid (HDCA) to BMSC dysfunction and the development of PMOP has not been elucidated. Objectives This study aimed to determine the role of HDCA in the metabolic regulation of BMSC homeostasis and to characterize its therapeutic potential and underlying molecular mechanisms in the context of PMOP. Methods Comprehensive serum bile acid profiling was performed in PMOP patients and healthy donors. Patient-derived BMSCs were treated with HDCA to evaluate its regulatory effects on senescence and lineage determination. The underlying molecular mechanisms involving the TGR5 (G protein‑coupled bile acid receptor 1)–ESR1 (Estrogen receptor 1) axis and mitochondrial quality control were explored through molecular docking, RNA sequencing, and pharmacological/genetic interventions, including the H 2 O 2 ‑induced senescence model, TGR5/ESR1 siRNA knockdown, PKA inhibition, and the ovariectomized (OVX) mouse model. Results Serum HDCA showed the largest reduction among the differential bile acids in PMOP patients, and its levels correlated negatively with BMSC senescence and adipogenesis. Exogenous HDCA treatment dose-dependently inhibited senescence and corrected aberrant adipogenesis in patient-derived BMSCs. Mechanistically, HDCA bound the membrane receptor TGR5 with higher affinity than for the nuclear farnesoid X receptor (FXR), activating a cAMP–PKA signaling cascade that upregulates ESR1 expression and triggers PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy to restore mitochondrial quality control. In OVX mice, oral HDCA administration replenished systemic HDCA levels, reversed bone architecture deterioration, and activated TGR5–ESR1 signaling in both intestinal and bone tissues. Conclusion HDCA supplementation alleviates BMSC senescence and aberrant adipogenesis through the TGR5–ESR1–mitophagy axis, providing a basis for the development of endogenous metabolite-based, non-hormonal strategies for PMOP.

title: Intestinal T-cell migration: unraveling mechanisms and therapeutic implications
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intestinal T-cell migration links mucosal immunity with systemic immune homeostasis and contributes to immune surveillance, barrier defense, and peripheral tissue inflammation. Advances in single-cell omics, spatial analysis, and intravital imaging are reshaping our understanding of its subset specificity and tissue selectivity. AIM OF REVIEW: This review summarizes the molecular mechanisms, microenvironmental regulation, pathological significance along the gut-organ axes, and related therapeutic strategies of intestinal T-cell migration, with a particular focus on how migratory imbalance contributes to intestinal and extraintestinal immune-mediated diseases. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS REVIEWED: Intestinal T-cell migration is jointly driven by gut imprinting, S1P-S1PR-mediated egress, chemokine-guided trafficking, integrin-dependent adhesion, and cytoskeletal remodeling, and is further regulated by metabolic, epigenetic, and microbial signals. This process is highly dependent on T-cell subset and tissue context: it promotes effector T-cell recruitment and inflammatory amplification in inflammatory bowel disease, manifests as restricted antitumor T-cell infiltration in colorectal cancer, and may contribute to distant tissue injury through the gut-organ axes. Existing S1PR modulators, integrin antagonists, and chemokine-targeted strategies have demonstrated the therapeutic tractability of migratory pathways; however, pathway redundancy, tissue heterogeneity, and impairment of protective immunity continue to limit their application. Future strategies should move beyond broad suppression of migration toward subset-, tissue-, and disease stage-specific precision modulation, combined with microbiota-based interventions and biomarker-guided stratification to improve therapeutic efficacy.

title: Rhizosphere Penicillium and phosphorus availability drive bioactive compound accumulation in Amomum villosum
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Amomum villosum (A. villosum), a medicinal herb rich in bioactive metabolites (borneol, bornyl acetate), exhibits superior quality in its core production region Yangchun (YC). However, the key habitat factors influencing the quality of A. villosum, as well as the underlying mechanisms, remain unclear. METHODS: This study employed an integrated multi-omics approach, incorporating metabolomics, transcriptomics, soil physicochemical property analysis, and metagenomics, to systematically compare the core production region with non-core regions. By identifying potential factors influencing regional disparities and validating the functional roles of key biotic and abiotic soil components through multi-level experimental designs, this research aimed to elucidate the primary determinants of product quality and their underlying regulatory mechanisms. RESULTS: The accumulation of major bioactive components, such as borneol and bornyl acetate, was significantly enhanced in YC A. villosum. Transcriptomic analyses showed that YC A. villosum exhibited preferential gene expression patterns, and further identified a functional gene (WvBAHD3) associated with bornyl acetate synthesis. Furthermore, we analyzed the physicochemical properties of soils from the four regions and revealed that available phosphorus (AP) were more abundant in YC soils than the other three non-core regions. Metagenomic analysis revealed that Penicillium, Limnoraphis, and Alcaligenes species were the dominant rhizosphere microorganisms, showing significant enrichment in YC soils compared to other regions. Correlation analysis indicated significant associations among the three dominant microorganisms, soil AP, and the accumulation of major bioactive components in A. villosum. We further isolated a fungus strain, Penicillium citrinum, and demonstrated its role in promoting the release of soil AP by secreting organic acids. Additionally, soil AP was confirmed to enhance the accumulation of bornyl acetate in A. villosum by upregulating the expression of regulatory genes. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that the recruitment of Penicillium species modulates bioactive compound accumulation in A. villosum via improved phosphorus availability, providing key guidance for high-quality cultivation of A. villosum.

title: Association of protein signature of fine particulate matter with MASLD: the underlying pathways and Mendelian randomization analysis
abstract: Introduction MASLD is a common chronic liver disease worldwide; identifying modifiable risk factors is crucial. Although fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) has been epidemiologically linked to MASLD, its mechanism remains unclear. Objectives To explore the mediating role of protein signature on the association between PM 2.5 and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and the underlying biological pathways. Methods We included 52,190 participants free of MASLD at baseline of a large cohort. Annual average PM 2.5 exposure was estimated by bilinear interpolation, and time-weighted method. PM 2.5 -related protein signature was constructed by elastic net regression, and KEGG/GO enrichment analysis was performed to identify potential pathways. Cox models were used to evaluate the associations of PM 2.5 and the protein signature with incident MASLD. Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was applied to examine potential causality between proteins and MASLD. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to the evaluate statistical mediation involving the protein and metabolic signatures. Results During a median follow-up of 11.8 years, 624 incident MASLD cases were identified. The PM 2.5 -related protein signature comprised 700 proteins, which were mainly enriched in pathways including NF-κB signaling pathway, and cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction. Both PM 2.5 exposure, and protein signature were significantly associated with incident MASLD, with hazard ratios (95 % confidence intervals) of 1.19 (1.10, 1.30), and 1.19 (1.08, 1.31). MR analysis provided genetic evidence supporting that CD28, CSF3 and HAVCR2 were associated with MASLD. Mediation analysis indicated that PM 2.5 -related protein signature mediated 15 % (95 % CI: 2.7 %, 37.7 %) of the PM 2.5 -MASLD association. SEM further suggested that PM 2.5 -related protein signature might mediate the PM 2.5 -MASLD association by regulating metabolic signatures. Conclusions The PM 2.5 -related protein signature was associated with MASLD, and showed statistical mediation of PM 2.5 -MASLD association potentially involving inflammatory and metabolic pathways.

title: A dual-bioeffect nanoengineered piezoelectric-photothermal hydrogel induces endochondral ossification and promotes critical-sized bone regeneration
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Critical-sized bone defects remain a major clinical challenge in orthopedics. Current strategies including inert implants and autologous bone grafts suffer from complications like loosening, infection, and donor site morbidity. Piezoelectric and photothermal stimuli synergistically regulate bone regeneration, and black phosphorus nanosheets (BPNSs) possess both effects and biodegradability, but are prone to oxidation and aggregation. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to develop an injectable biomimetic hydrogel with dual piezoelectric-photothermal bioeffects for minimally invasive and efficient repair of irregular critical-sized bone defects. METHODS: BPNS@rhCOL1MA composite system was constructed by embedding BPNSs into recombinant human methacrylated type I collagen hydrogel. Physicochemical characterization, in vitro cell assays, transcriptomic analysis, and in vivo validation in a rabbit rib defect model were performed. RESULTS: The material exhibited stable network, injectability, and controllable dual-responsive properties. It significantly enhanced osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs in vitro. Transcriptomics revealed activation of electrical/thermal signal transduction and angiogenesis pathways. In vivo, it markedly improved new bone formation, bone mineral density, and mechanical properties. CONCLUSION: This work first integrates the dual bioeffects of BPNSs with injectable human-derived collagen hydrogel, providing a novel strategy for minimally invasive repair of irregular bone defects.

title: Advanced nanocarrier delivery and therapeutic systems for natural drug molecules: mechanisms, applications and future perspectives
abstract: BACKGROUND: Natural drug molecules often face challenges such as poor water solubility and low bioavailability, which limit their clinical efficacy. Nanocarrier technology offers a promising strategy to address these bottlenecks by improving solubility, protecting active ingredients, and enabling targeted delivery. AIM: of Review: This review systematically surveys the state-of-the-art progress of diverse nanocarrier systems for the delivery of natural drug molecules. It uniquely emphasizes the rational design of nanocarriers, the elucidation of molecular-level interaction mechanisms between natural drugs and nanocarriers, and strategies for achieving specific target recognition and controlled release. Key Scientific Concepts of Review: This review illustrates how the strategic design of various nanocarriers can overcome the inherent physicochemical and biopharmaceutical limitations of natural drug molecules. By elucidating their interaction mechanisms, this review provides an essential foundation for the rational design of nanocarrier-natural drug systems. Furthermore, it critically analyzes translational bottlenecks such as biocompatibility and scalable manufacturing and proposes future directions for next-generation nanocarrier platforms by integrating cutting-edge interdisciplinary approaches, including multistimuli-responsive systems, AI-driven design, and biomimetic strategies.

title: A Mir338-CDK8-mitochondrial axis governs lineage-specific osteogenesis and defines Runx2 pleiotropy in cranial sutures
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Developmental pattern formation critically depends on gene regulatory networks that enable context-dependent interpretation of molecular cues, yet how cells from distinct embryonic lineages in shared microenvironments produce divergent outcomes remains a central unresolved question. The murine skull provides a key model: the neural crest-derived posterior frontal (PF) suture fuses, while the mesoderm-derived sagittal (SAG) suture remains patent. A recently identified paradox exists: Runx2 haploinsufficiency impacts both sutures, but Mir338 cluster ablation selectively rescues the SAG suture, suggesting lineage-specific regulatory constraints. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to resolve this paradox by investigating how embryonic origin dictates osteoprogenitor responses to Runx2-Mir338 signaling. METHODS: We employed multi-omics (miRNA-seq, RNA-seq, scRNA-seq) and lineage tracing to define transcriptional heterogeneity, dissect Runx2 and Mir338-mediated lineage-specific regulation of osteoblastic subclusters, and identify differentially expressed mitochondrial-related genes and Cyclin-dependent kinase 8 (Cdk8). These findings were functionally validated through in vivo and in vitro assays. RESULTS: We uncover that embryonic origin dictates osteoprogenitor responses to Runx2-Mir338 signaling through lineage-specific mitochondrial dynamics. In mesoderm-derived SAG sutures, Runx2 haploinsufficiency disrupts mitochondrial fragmentation, a process critical for ossification, via dysregulation of NADH: ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit S5 (NDUFS5). We identify CDK8 as a novel direct target of Mir338 and a Runx2-activated gene that promotes mitochondrial fragmentation. This dual regulation of CDK8 establishes a dosage-sensitive "toggle switch" unique to SAG sutures, where restoring mitochondrial function via direct mitochondrial transplantation rescues ossification defects. In contrast, neural crest-derived PF sutures exhibit intrinsically low CDK8 expression, partially modulated by DNA methylation, rendering them unresponsive to Runx2-Mir338 modulation and mitochondrial rescue. CONCLUSION: Our findings resolve the paradox of Runx2 pleiotropy by bridging positional identity, mitochondrial metabolism, and miRNA-mediated regulation, offering a redefined conceptual framework for understanding developmental processes and informing precision therapeutic strategies for congenital skeletal disorders.

title: Corrigendum to “Maximizing crustaceans (shrimp, crab, and lobster) by-products value for optimum valorization practices: A comparative review of their active ingredients, extraction, bioprocesses and applications” [J. Adv. Res. 57 (2024) 59–76]
Network toxicology, machine learning, single-cell analysis, and molecular docking reveal 6PPD/6PPD-Q-associated atrial fibrillation signatures
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent sustained arrhythmia worldwide, and environmental factors are increasingly recognized as contributors to its complex pathogenesis. The tire antioxidant N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD) and its oxidation product 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) are emerging environmental contaminants with reported cardiotoxicity; however, their molecular relationship with AF remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify potential molecular targets and pathways that link 6PPD/6PPD-Q exposure to AF using an integrated network toxicology and machine learning strategy. METHODS: Multicohort atrial microarray datasets from patients with AF were integrated to identify AF-related genes using differential expression analysis, weighted gene coexpression network analysis, and GeneCards database screening. Putative targets of 6PPD/6PPD-Q were predicted using multiple in silico databases and intersected with AF-related genes. Network toxicology, enrichment analysis, machine learning with SHAP interpretation, single-cell RNA sequencing, and molecular docking were utilized to identify and characterize hub genes. Key targets were validated using qRT-PCR and western blotting in human cardiac fibroblasts. A mouse exposure model was further used to assess AF inducibility, duration, and cardiac gene expression in vivo. RESULTS: Sixteen putative AF-associated target genes of 6PPD/6PPD-Q were identified. Machine learning analysis highlighted four hub genes as key candidate hubs. Single-cell RNA analysis revealed cell type-specific expression, with enrichment in cardiomyocytes and vascular structural cells. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding interactions between 6PPD/6PPD-Q and the key target proteins. In vitro exposure to 6PPD or 6PPD-Q at the tested concentrations upregulated the mRNA and protein levels of all four candidate genes. In vivo exposure significantly increased pacing-induced AF inducibility, prolonged AF duration, and upregulated the expression of all these genes in cardiac tissues. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that 6PPD and 6PPD-Q may contribute to AF by targeting specific genes and signaling pathways, with DDR1, BCHE, HTR2B, and KCNJ3 identified as core exposure-related hubs.

title: Association between dental pulp necroptosis-related signaling and elodont incisor growth retardation in hyperglycemic rats
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Although type 1 diabetes (T1D) induces systemic allostatic load, whether sustained hyperglycemia is accompanied by necroptosis-related signaling within the dental pulp (DP) niche and its impact on the developmental kinetics of continuously growing elodont incisors remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: This study investigated whether sustained hyperglycemia was accompanied by enhanced RIPK3-MLKL necroptosis-related signaling within the DP niche and whether these molecular alterations coincided with attenuation of elodont incisor growth. METHODS: T1D was induced in Sprague-Dawley rats using streptozotocin (65 mg/kg). Systemic metabolic profiles, necroptotic markers in serum/dental tissues (immunohistochemistry, ELISA, and Western blotting), and mandibular incisor growth (a standardized notch-creation method for 49 days) were evaluated. Group differences were assessed primarily using two-sided Welch's t-tests, with exact Mann-Whitney U tests for sensitivity analyses, while discriminative performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC-AUC) and precision-recall (PR curve-based AP) analyses. RESULTS: Hyperglycemic rats exhibited impaired weight gain, systemic inflammatory induction (elevated NLR/MLR), and elevated hepatic stress markers. Molecular profiling demonstrated increased oxidative damage (4-HNE) and necroptosis-related molecular alterations in dental tissues and DP-derived cells. Incisor growth rates differed significantly at the Phase-Transition (0.532 vs. 0.400 mm/day; Welch's p = 0.024), reaching definitive retardation in Phase-2 (0.594 vs. 0.408 mm/day; p < 0.001). Discriminatory performance improved from the Phase-Transition (ROC-AUC = 0.693; AP = 0.784) to Phase-2 (ROC-AUC = 1.000; AP = 1.000). Glycemic reversion was accompanied by normalization of necroptosis-related markers and incisor growth kinetics. CONCLUSION: Hyperglycemia-induced incisor growth retardation is associated with increased oxidative stress, altered PGAM5 expression, and enhanced RIPK3-MLKL necroptosis-related signaling in dental tissues and DP-derived cells. Translationally, longitudinal evaluation of elodont incisor growth kinetics could serve as a minimally invasive phenotypic indicator of metabolic dysregulation in preclinical diabetic models and support refinement under the 3Rs principle.

title: Identifying overlooked factors associated with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis: an ecological study across 201 countries and regions, 1990–2021
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is a critical global health challenge. Whether environmental, nutritional, and socioeconomic factors are associated with MDR-TB remains insufficiently investigated. METHODS: We analyzed outcome and exposure data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study and four additional databases covering 201 countries and territories from 1990 to 2021; the primary analyses included 4,019 country-years from 186 countries. Sex ratio, diabetes prevalence, and HIV/AIDS burden were regressed out of each outcome before analysis. Every candidate exposure was then both regressed against the confounder-adjusted outcome and correlated with it. Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values, together with correlation strength, determined which factors were retained for display. Effects are expressed as the absolute change per interquartile range (IQR) increase in exposure. Drug-susceptible tuberculosis served as a control outcome. RESULTS: Per IQR of exposure, unsafe sanitation was associated with 13.9 more prevalent cases per 100,000 (95% CI 13.0-14.7) and 2.87 more deaths per 100,000 (2.72-3.03); unsafe water source with 11.2 (10.5-12.0) and 2.64 (2.49-2.78); and polluting fuels for cooking with 10.7 (9.8-11.6) and 2.74 (2.58-2.89). After further adjustment for GDP per capita and health expenditure, six of the thirteen principal exposures remained significantly associated with MDR-TB prevalence, including unsafe sanitation, unsafe water source, absence of handwashing facilities and underweight (e.g., unsafe sanitation 2.8 per 100,000 per IQR, P < 0.001). Most of these associations were stronger for drug-susceptible disease than for MDR-TB, with the exception of diet low in fruits. CONCLUSIONS: Unsafe sanitation, unsafe water source, and polluting fuels for cooking are the population-level factors most strongly associated with MDR-TB burden. These associations are largely shared with drug-susceptible tuberculosis, supporting their integration into tuberculosis control efforts as a whole.

title: Psyllid glycine-rich antimicrobial peptides oligomerize to directly cleave zinc transporter ZnuA on the membranes of citrus Huanglongbing pathogen
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Huanglongbing (HLB), the most devastating citrus disease worldwide, is caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas) and transmitted by Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri. Currently, the potential role of the insect vector's innate immunity against CLas remains poorly understood. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify and characterize a 41-amino acid glycine-rich antimicrobial peptide from D. citri (DcGrAMP1), elucidate its molecular mechanism against CLas and related α-proteobacteria, and evaluate its efficacy in suppressing CLas in HLB-affected citrus under greenhouse and field conditions. METHODS: Through genomic screening and CLas-induced expression validation, we obtained DcGrAMP1; combined with structural prediction, site-directed mutagenesis, molecular interaction techniques, and RNA interference, we elucidated its mechanism against CLas and regulatory pathway; through transgenic citrus construction and protein injection assays, we validated its CLas-suppressive efficacy under greenhouse and field conditions. RESULTS: DcGrAMP1 exhibits remarkable thermal stability. It oligomerizes through Arg26/Arg31 for bacterial membrane penetration, and Arg21 engages in binding-associated cleavage upon interacting with Asp153 of zinc transporter ZnuA on CLas membranes, thereby cleaving the adjacent peptide bond and triggering ZnuA degradation. CLas infection activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase-activator protein 1 (JNK-AP1) signaling pathway in the psyllid, thereby upregulating DcGrAMP1 expression. Overexpression or injection of DcGrAMP1 in citrus significantly reduced CLas titers and alleviated HLB symptoms. CONCLUSION: This work provides the evidence that insect AMPs can oligomerize to penetrate CLas membranes, and then directly cleave zinc transporter ZnuA on the membranes of citrus Huanglongbing pathogen.

title: Zinc peroxide-coated gold nanorods as the therapeutic adjuvants for photothermal enhanced chemodynamic therapy and metalloimmunotherapy against tumor
abstract: Introduction Traditional tumor therapies have limited efficacy, leading to a high mortality rate. Although immunotherapy holds considerable therapeutic promise, clinical immunotherapy for solid tumors only elicits durable responses in a minority of patients. This limitation is largely attributed to the highly immunosuppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Notably, conventional chemodynamic therapy (CDT) is hampered by endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) shortage in tumor cells, and AZP compensates this defect via in-situ H 2 O 2 self-supplementation to amplify hydroxyl radical generation. Objectives To develop a nanoplatform capable of systematically enhancing anti-tumor immunity, we rationally constructed a PEGylated zinc peroxide-coated gold nanorod (AZP) as a therapeutic adjuvant with acid-responsive properties for the combination therapy of cancer. Methods Gold nanorod-based adjuvants coated with zinc peroxide were successfully prepared via chemical oxidation, followed by PEGylation. The morphology and size of the AZP were characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and hydrodynamic diameter measurements. The elemental composition of AZP was determined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analysis. The acid-responsive degradation and photothermally enhanced catalytic properties of AZP were evaluated using TEM, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, absorption spectroscopy, and thermal imaging tracing. The therapeutic mechanism of AZP at the cellular level was investigated through a series of experiments, including TEM, fluorescence imaging, immunofluorescence assays, Seahorse analysis, western blotting, and bioinformatics approaches, which comprehensively clarified the anti-tumor mechanism of AZP. Bilateral tumor and metastatic tumor models were established to verify the anti-tumor efficacy and mechanism of AZP at the animal level. Specifically, fluorescence imaging, immunofluorescence staining, tissue staining analysis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and flow cytometry were performed to assess the in vivo therapeutic effects. Results In the acidic TME, the AZP nanoplatform releases H 2 O 2 and zinc ions, which increases the reactive oxygen species level in cancer cells. Additionally, due to its photothermally enhanced peroxidase-like activity, AZP induces the generation of more hydroxyl radicals under light irradiation. These effects synergistically disrupt lysosomes and mitochondria in tumor cells, block autophagy, and ultimately lead to tumor cell death. Furthermore, zinc supplementation by AZP enhances the activation of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase and stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Meanwhile, the combined treatment induces immunogenic cell death of cancer cells, which promotes the release of tumor-associated antigens and activates robust anti-tumor immune responses. Notably, intratumoral injection of the AZP adjuvant combined with irradiation effectively eradicates in situ tumors. When further combined with PD-1 antibody, this regimen can induce anti-tumor immunity, significantly inhibiting tumor growth, metastasis, and recurrence in a murine model without causing obvious toxicity. Conclusion The AZP nanoplatform exhibits excellent therapeutic efficacy, providing a rational design strategy for a potent adjuvant that integrates photothermally enhanced chemodynamic therapy and metalloimmunotherapy for the treatment of solid tumors.

title: Mitophagy and ER-phagy in doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity: mechanisms, crosstalk, and therapeutic implications
abstract: BACKGROUND: Doxorubicin (DOX) is a key chemotherapeutic agent for hematologic malignancies and many solid tumors, but its clinical use is limited by doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity (DIC). DIC may present as subclinical myocardial injury, arrhythmias, left ventricular dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, or heart failure. DOX can disrupt organelle function through topoisomerase IIβ (Top2β)-mediated DNA damage and transcriptional stress, oxidative stress, disrupted iron homeostasis, and calcium imbalance. Mitochondrial and endoplasmic/sarcoplasmic reticulum (ER/SR) injury are therefore central pathological features of DIC. AIM OF REVIEW: This review summarizes current evidence on mitophagy and ER-phagy in DIC, with emphasis on discrepancies in reported findings across different experimental settings, potential crosstalk mechanisms, and the translational limitations of targeting these pathways for cardioprotection. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS: Current studies suggest that mitophagy in DIC follows a checkpoint-dependent pattern. Depending on DOX dose, exposure duration, and lysosomal degradative capacity, mitophagy may remove damaged mitochondria, but it may also worsen mitochondrial injury when initiation is insufficient, activation is excessive, or flux is stalled. In contrast, direct evidence for ER-phagy in DIC remains limited. This evidence is mainly derived from CCPG1-mediated protective ER-phagy in chronic fractionated DOX models and FAM134B-associated ER-phagy-related injury signals in acute high-dose injury models. Thus, the functional divergence of ER-phagy in DIC requires confirmation in additional experimental models with rigorous autophagic flux assessment. Mitochondria-associated ER membranes (MAMs) may coordinate mitophagy and ER-phagy by regulating calcium transfer, autophagosome formation, and receptor localization. Overall, current evidence does not support indiscriminate activation or inhibition of mitophagy and ER-phagy. Instead, future interventions may need to preserve flux-complete organelle clearance while avoiding excessive or stalled autophagic signaling. In addition, this framework may help generate research hypotheses that integrate cardioprotection with preservation of antitumor efficacy. However, most evidence comes from cell and animal studies, and further validation in human myocardial tissue and confirmation of cardiac target engagement are still needed.

title: Recent advances in research on the association between lactylation and regulated cell death in sepsis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction mediated by host immune dysregulation, and elevated serum lactate levels are an important pathophysiological feature. Lactate is not only the terminal product of glucose metabolism but also acts as a signaling molecule that regulates gene expression and protein function through lactylation. Regulated cell death (RCD), as a targetable terminal cell fate, offers a potential direction for precision intervention in sepsis. OBJECTIVE: Although studies have indicated that lactylation can affect sepsis progression by regulating RCD, no review has systematically summarized this relationship. Therefore, this review systematically summarizes the regulatory roles of lactylation in RCD and their pathological significance in sepsis. INNOVATION: Based on the above evidence, this review proposes that "lactylation modification imbalance-aberrant activation of RCD" may be a potential driving mechanism of sepsis progression and that the lactylation/acetylation imbalance caused by glucose metabolism reprogramming is an upstream regulatory link of this axis. CONCLUSION: In summary, targeting lactylation modification to precisely modulate RCD may interrupt the pathological chain from lactate elevation to organ injury, providing new perspectives for sepsis treatment research.

title: Corrigendum to “Longitudinal prediction of drug response in high-grade serous ovarian cancer organoid cultures aligning with clinical responses” [J. Adv. Res. 83 (2026) 379–390]
A novel framework for identifying cellular signature LncRNAs and their functional coregulatory networks with prognostic implications at single-cell resolution
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Long non-coding RNAs have been implicated in crucial roles in developing malignant tumors. However, comprehensive analyses of lncRNA within the tumor microenvironment, particularly at the single-cell level across various tumor types, remain limited. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to establish a comprehensive methodological framework for prioritizing and identifying novel cancer-associated lncRNA biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets at the single-cell level, and to integrate these findings into a unified platform. METHODS: We developed SIGLNCOS, a computational framework for analyzing single-cell lncRNA regulation via: i) Constructing the lncRNA visualization landscape. ii) Identifying cellular signature lncRNA. iii) Functional enrichment of clncRNAs. iv) Identifying co-lncRNA pairs based on shared functional annotations and weighted functional association scores. Cell-composition-adjusted prognostic analysis evaluated the prognostic relevance of individual lncRNAs and co-lncRNA pairs. RESULTS: Applying SIGLNCOS, we identified 667 cellular-signature lncRNAs (clncRNAs) from over half a million single cells across 31 cancers, revealing their roles in immune modulation, tumor progression, and differentiation. NEAT1 was associated with distinct macrophage states and functional changes along pseudotime. SIGLNCOS identified 3,381 co-lncRNA pairs involved in key cancer-related pathways, revealing a complex landscape of lncRNA co-regulation. Notably, we uncovered distinct co-lncRNA networks associated with different thyroid cancer states, particularly between papillary thyroid carcinoma and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. These networks exhibit functionally concordant regulatory effects that individual lncRNAs cannot, underscoring the importance of co-regulation in tumor evolution. The prognostic analysis demonstrated that co-lncRNA networks outperform individual lncRNAs in predicting patient outcomes, emphasizing their potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets. CONCLUSION: This study constructs pan-cancer lncRNA landscapes and develops SIGLNCOS, a comprehensive framework for uncovering lncRNA at single-cell resolution, offering new insights into cancer biology and potential avenues for targeted therapies and novel biomarker discovery. We further developed sCo-Lnc (https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/scolnc), a web-based platform for visualizing novel lncRNA biomarkers across cancers.

title: EZH2 lactylation: a key epigenetic regulator and potential therapeutic target for sepsis-associated lung injury
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sepsis-associated lung injury (SALI) is a lethal infection-induced complication with high mortality and limited targeted therapies. Dysregulated lactate metabolism is closely linked to SALI, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the role and molecular mechanism of EZH2 (Enhancer of zeste homolog 2) lactylation in SALI development, thereby uncovering a novel exploitable therapeutic target. METHODS: ) mouse models were established. Combined with lactate and lactate dehydrogenase inhibitor intervention, multi-omics analysis, ChIP, qPCR, immunofluorescence and other techniques were used in the study. RESULTS: Serum lactate levels were significantly elevated in patients with SALI and model mice, and lung tissue lactate levels were elevated in model mice. Lactate levels were positively associated with inflammatory markers and lung injury severity. EZH2 underwent site-specific lactylation at lysine 30 and 406 (EZH2 K30/K406la) in SALI, which was enhanced with disease progression. Inhibiting lactate production or EZH2 lactylation improved pulmonary function, reduced inflammatory infiltration and pathological lung tissue damage. EZH2 K30/K406la downregulated CITED2 (CBP-p300 interacting transactivator with Glu/Asp-rich carboxy-terminal domain 2) expression by reducing its occupancy at the CITED2 promoter and altering CITED2 promoter activity, relieving the inhibition of the NF-κB (Nuclear Factor-kappa B) pathway and exacerbating inflammatory responses and endothelial dysfunction. CONCLUSION: EZH2 lactylation aggravates SALI via the CITED2/NF-κB axis, highlighting this epigenetic modification as a promising therapeutic target that opens a new pharmacological avenue for developing site-specific inhibitors to combat SALI.

title: Simultaneous brain–spinal fMRI reveals neural mechanisms of TENS-induced analgesia
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) can produce analgesia, but its associated cortical, brainstem, and spinal response patterns in humans remain incompletely understood. OBJECTIVES: To compare the analgesic effects and associated brain-spinal response patterns of two TENS protocols: high-frequency/low-intensity and low-frequency/high-intensity stimulation. METHODS: Ninety-two healthy adults were randomized to high-frequency TENS, low-frequency TENS, or sham stimulation. Bilateral heat-pain responses were assessed using simultaneous brain-spinal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) before and after a 30-min intervention. Pain ratings, regional activation, and periaqueductal gray (PAG)-centered functional connectivity were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with correction for multiple comparisons. RESULTS: The two TENS protocols produced different spatial profiles of analgesia. High-frequency/low-intensity TENS produced treated-side analgesia relative to sham for pain intensity (β = -2.57, 95 % confidence interval [CI] [-3.26, -1.87]) and unpleasantness (β = -2.53, 95 % CI [-3.51, -1.55]). Treated-side analgesia was accompanied by reduced heat-evoked activity in the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), PAG, rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), and C6 spinal cord, increased ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity, and altered PAG-spinal connectivity. Low-frequency/high-intensity TENS produced bilateral analgesia, reducing pain intensity on the treated and untreated sides (β = -2.07 and -1.75, respectively) and unpleasantness (β = -1.98 and -1.70, respectively). This bilateral effect was accompanied by reduced activity in primary somatosensory cortex (S1)/dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)/supplementary motor area (SMA), S2, and spinal cord, together with PAG-S1 and PAG-spinal connectivity changes. CONCLUSION: TENS analgesia was associated with protocol-specific brain-spinal response patterns. High-frequency/low-intensity TENS produced localized analgesia with neural changes consistent with spinal and supraspinal modulation, whereas low-frequency/high-intensity TENS produced bilateral analgesia with broader PAG-sensorimotor-spinal involvement.

title: PPAR-γ/SGK1/GSK3β/Nrf2 signaling pathway contributes to the neuroprotective effects of lycopene in depressed mice
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a neuropsychiatric disorder associated with abnormal neuronal activity in specific brain regions. Recent evidence suggests that oxidative stress- and neuroinflammation-driven impairments in synaptic structure and neuronal function may contribute to depression, yet the precise mechanisms remain unclear. Lycopene (LYC) is a lipophilic dietary carotenoid that exhibits strong neuroprotective and antioxidant properties. OBJECTIVES: Here, we report that LYC alleviates chronic stress-induced neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and impaired synaptic transmission by activating the PPAR-γ/SGK1/p-GSK3β/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling pathway. METHODS AND RESULTS: Integrated transcriptomic and network pharmacology analyses prioritized PPAR-γ as a potential target of LYC. Moreover, pharmacological activation of PPAR-γ induced LYC-like effects by alleviating chronic stress-induced behavioral deficiency, oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, whereas CA1-local inhibition of PPAR-γ weakened LYC-mediated neuroprotection effects. Electrophysiological data further suggest that chronic stress weakened synaptic transmission and excitability in CA1 pyramidal neurons, while LYC improved the neuronal dysfunction through a PPAR-γ/SGK1/p-GSK3β/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate that LYC activates the PPAR-γ/SGK1/p-GSK3β/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling pathway to alleviate chronic stress-induced oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, thereby improving neuroplasticity and protecting against stress-related depression.

title: Deciphering conserved and divergent tissue architectures via soDGVAE-mediated spatial transcriptomics integration
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spatial omics has revolutionized our understanding of molecular heterogeneity within its native tissue context. However, the integrative analysis of datasets spanning replicate samples, disparate platforms, different developmental stages, and cross-species remains a challenging computational task. OBJECTIVES: Here, we present soDGVAE, a conditional graph attention variational autoencoder framework engineered for the robust harmonization and alignment of multisource spatial transcriptomics data. METHODS: By synergistically encoding gene expression and spatial topology through a graph attention variational autoencoder, soDGVAE effectively decouples technical batch effects from genuine biological variation. RESULTS: Through comprehensive benchmarking, we demonstrate that the proposed model performs competitively in integrating replicate samples across platforms, large-scale multi-technology atlases, and datasets with limited gene overlap. Beyond technical integration, soDGVAE facilitates deep biological discovery: it enables the high-fidelity domain identification in the three-dimensional murine kidney architecture, and distinguishes coarse and fine-grained regions in the developmental avian heart. Notably, the cross-species study found that in the same Carnegie stage, the skin of mice matured earlier than that of humans, which elucidates the heterogeneous shifts in developmental tempo across species. Finally, we applied soDGVAE to the kidney cohort to decode the key domains. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our results position soDGVAE as a scalable and generalizable tool, transforming discrete tissue slices into coherent, multi-dimensional biological maps.

title: CMTM6 regulates hematopoietic stem cell homeostasis through modulating IFNRs-STAT1-KLF4 signaling axis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: CMTM6 is known to stabilize PD-L1 on cancer cells, facilitating immune evasion, but its role in normal hematopoiesis remains unexplored. Hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) homeostasis is tightly regulated by interferon (IFN) signaling, yet the mechanisms controlling IFN receptor stability are unclear. OBJECTIVES: In this study we investigated whether CMTM6 regulates HSC maintenance and elucidated the underlying molecular pathways. METHODS: Using a conditional Cmtm6 knockout mouse model (Vav-Cre), we performed flow cytometry, competitive transplantation, single-cell RNA sequencing, co-immunoprecipitation, and functional assays on bone marrow HSCs. RESULTS: Cmtm6 deficiency led to increased HSC proliferation but impaired reconstitution capacity, accompanied by elevated DNA damage and disrupted cell polarity. Single-cell analysis revealed a marked reduction in IFN response pathways. Mechanistically, CMTM6 directly interacted with IFNAR1 and IFNGR1, stabilizing their protein expression. Downstream, Cmtm6 deletion impaired STAT1 phosphorylation and reduced KLF4 expression; single-cell analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between Stat1 activity and Klf4 expression, and STAT1 inhibition in HSCs confirmed that STAT1 activity is required for maintaining KLF4 expression. Notably, KLF4 overexpression partially rescued colony-forming defects and reduced γH2AX foci in Cmtm6-deficient HSCs, identifying KLF4 as a key downstream effector. Additionally, we observed accompanying molecular changes including reduced SIAH2, elevated DYRK2, decreased c-MYC, and increased P53, which may contribute to the observed phenotypes. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that CMTM6 maintains HSC homeostasis by stabilizing IFN receptors and regulating the IFNR-STAT1-KLF4 signaling axis, revealing a novel physiological function for CMTM6 in hematopoiesis.

title: Single-cell chromatin accessibility atlas decodes bone development, diseases, and regeneration
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bone development, homeostasis, and regeneration are governed by complex, dynamic gene regulatory programs, and these processes are disrupted in numerous skeletal diseases. The epigenetic landscape-particularly chromatin accessibility-dictates transcription factor binding and gene expression, which fundamentally shape bone cell fate and function. In recent years, single-cell chromatin accessibility technologies, most notably single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), have revolutionized bone epigenome research and enabled single-cell resolution dissection of the skeletal system. AIM OF REVIEW: This review summarizes recent progress in single-cell chromatin accessibility studies in bone biology, and systematically outlines chromatin-accessibility changes in skeletal development, diseases, and regeneration. We introduce cutting-edge single-cell epigenomic mapping technologies, their bone tissue-specific adaptations, and analytical frameworks for multi-omics data integration. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS OF REVIEW: These approaches reveal key biological findings: the identification of bone-resident subpopulations and lineage hierarchies, dynamic enhancer landscapes during osteoblast/chondrocyte differentiation, cellular bases of diseases such as osteoporosis and osteoarthritis, and novel mechanisms of bone tumorigenesis. Moreover, we discuss cross-applications of genomics and functional research, including mapping of disease-associated regulatory elements and emerging epigenome-editing strategies. Finally, we address current challenges, outline future directions, and envision the integration of single-cell epigenomics in precision orthopedics and regenerative medicine.

title: Estrogen-driven PDK4-MYH9 phosphorylation promotes mitochondrial fission and osteogenic commitment of mesenchymal stem cells
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMOP), driven primarily by estrogen deficiency, represents a major public health challenge. Although estrogen's anti-resorptive effects are well established, the direct osteogenic actions by which it regulates the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) remain poorly understood. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to elucidate a novel mechanism by which estrogen regulates osteogenic differentiation in MSCs and to identify key downstream molecular events. METHODS: We employed single-cell RNA sequencing to profile the transcriptional landscape of osteoporotic MSCs. The pro-osteogenic effects of estradiol (E2) were validated in ovariectomized mice and primary mouse bone marrow-derived MSCs through in vitro differentiation assays and mitochondrial functional analyses. Downstream targets of estrogen receptor were identified by integrating CUT&Tag-seq with transcriptomic data and validated using conditional knockout mice. Protein interactions and phosphorylation sites were mapped via co-immunoprecipitation, mass spectrometry, site-directed mutagenesis, and mitochondrial morphology assays. RESULTS: Osteoporotic MSCs displayed concurrent impairments in osteogenic differentiation and mitochondrial function. E2 stimulated mitochondrial fission, enhanced maximal respiration, and induced DRP1 translocation to mitochondria. The combined evidence from our CUT&Tag-seq, RNA-seq, and the additional CUT&Tag-qPCR and ERα knockdown data supports the conclusion that Pdk4 is a direct transcriptional target of ERα. This finding is further corroborated by the compromised osteogenesis observed in conditional Pdk4 knockout mice.
