Mechanistically, PDK4 catalyzed MYH9 phosphorylation at serine 1943, thereby facilitating DRP1 recruitment to mitochondria and subsequent fission. Both pharmacological inhibition of PDK4 and introduction of the phosphorylation-deficient MYH9 S1943A mutant abolished the E2-induced effects. Notably, Pdk4 overexpression in ovariectomized mice reversed bone loss in the absence of exogenous estrogen. CONCLUSION: This study identifies an unrecognized ERα-PDK4-MYH9 signaling axis through which estrogen drives mitochondrial fission to promote osteogenic differentiation of MSCs. These findings expand the current understanding of estrogen's skeletal actions by revealing a pro-osteogenic effect on MSCs, and suggest PDK4 as a potential candidate for therapeutic exploration in PMOP.

title: Development and multicenter validation of a cfDNA methylation-based PCR assay (myESCAP) with machine-learning prediction for non-invasive detection of esophageal cancer
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Esophageal cancer (EC) remains a significant public health burden in China. Current diagnostics modalities such as endoscopy and imaging are invasive, poorly accessible, or insensitive for early-stage cases. DNA methylation alterations in circulating free DNA (cfDNA) are promising for non-invasive cancer detection. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to develop and validate a methylation PCR-based assay for EC detection using EC-specific DNA methylation targets. Here, we report myESCAP, a PCR-based assay that amplifies and quantifies levels of EC-specific methylation in cfDNA METHODS: We conducted a multi-center, retrospective case-control study with 489 EC cases and 555 non-malignant controls (benign esophageal/gastric diseases or asymptomatic) to develop myESCAP, a methylation-specific PCR assay containing 11 EC-specific methylation markers from our previous genome-wide methylation screening, selected for strong discriminative performance and PCR compatibility. cfDNA was collected, bisulfite-converted, and tested by myESCAP, and results were analyzed by six modeling strategies (generalized linear model, k-nearest neighbors, C5.0 decision tree, gradient boosting machine, random forest, support vector machine) to train EC-prediction models using 347 EC cases and 349 non-malignant controls, and validated in 142 EC cases and 206 controls. RESULTS: . The six models showed robust performance in the training cohort (average AUC = 0.835, average sensitivity = 76.13%, average specificity = 90.88%). They maintained performance in the validation cohort (average AUC = 0.823, average sensitivity = 75.59%, average specificity = 89%). Specifically, for stage I cases, myESCAP had an average sensitivity of 47.2%, highlighting the challenge of early detection with limited circulating tumor DNA and the need for further optimization. CONCLUSION: myESCAP accurately differentiated EC from non-malignant controls. The six models collectively confirm myESCAP's robustness and clinical potential as a cost-effective, non-invasive diagnostic tool for EC.

title: Multi-objective particle swarm optimization with prior-posterior knowledge guidance and hybrid environmental selection for feature selection
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Multi-objective feature selection (MOFS) aims to select compact feature subsets while maintaining classification accuracy. For high-dimensional data, traditional multi-objective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) is often limited by random initialization, weak binary-space exploitation, and biased environmental selection during evolutionary search. OBJECTIVES: This study proposes an improved MOPSO framework to better balance classification accuracy and subset sparsity while maintaining convergence, diversity, and search efficiency. METHODS: We propose MOPSO_PPHS, a MOPSO-based framework integrating prior-posterior knowledge guidance, a V-shaped transfer operator, and hybrid environmental selection. Unlike methods relying mainly on static feature scores or elite Pareto solutions, the proposed guidance mechanism combines filter-based prior information with evolution-derived posterior feedback to support sparse initialization and feature-level mutation. The V-shaped operator improves binary position updating, while the hybrid environmental selection strategy preserves sparse and accurate boundary solutions to maintain Pareto-front coverage. Experiments were conducted on 20 benchmark datasets against eight representative algorithms using HV, IGD, MER, and ART. RESULTS: MOPSO_PPHS achieves the best average ranks on HV and IGD among the compared algorithms, indicating better convergence and Pareto-front coverage. It obtains low MER on high-dimensional datasets, with zero classification error on several datasets, while maintaining low ART. CONCLUSION: MOPSO_PPHS improves traditional MOPSO by combining knowledge-guided search, binary-space search enhancement, and boundary-aware environmental selection. The proposed framework provides an effective approach for high-dimensional MOFS, with potential use in medical gene screening and related high-dimensional classification tasks.

title: From discovery to engineering: revealing and optimizing the indigoids biosynthesis by FMO from Indigofera tinctoria
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Indigo-producing plants have been used for millennia as natural dyes and traditional medicines. Despite evolutionary divergence, these species converge on a conserved indigo biosynthesis pathway, yet the molecular basis for differences in catalytic efficiency remains largely unknown. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify and characterize the key genes involved in indigoid biosynthesisfrom Indigofera tinctoria, and to elucidate the structural determinants underlying their catalytic properties. METHODS: We performed transcriptome mining and functional screening of candidate genes fromI. tinctoria, followed by enzyme kinetic characterization, substrate specificity profiling, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the catalytically competent state, alanine scanning mutagenesis, and metabolic engineering through co-expression and co-cultivation strategies in Escherichia coli. RESULTS: ) toward indole than other plant FMOs tested, and converted 16 substituted indoles into variously colored indigoids. When 2-oxindole was supplied, ItFMO co-produced indirubin (∼70% of total pigments) via condensation of enzymatically generated indoxyl with 2-oxindole. Co-expression of ItFMO with E. coli TnaA (Tryptophanase) yielded the highest indigo titer (41.27 ± 0.84 mg/L), followed by ItINS (30.54 ± 0.33 mg/L) and ItFMO alone (27.58 ± 0.19 mg/L), whereas ItTSA severely reduced production (5.68 ± 0.20 mg/L). Co-cultivation of the two strains achieved a 2.7-fold increase over the monoculture, with a titer of 60.03 ± 0.82 mg/L. MD simulations and alanine scanning identified Q51, Y160, K212, S213, F373, and N427 as critical residues governing ItFMO catalysis, and which were authenticated by site-directed mutagenesis. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish a mechanistic basis for understanding FMO-mediated indigo formation in plants and provide a structural insight for engineering plant-derived enzymes in microbial systems.

title: Transcriptome and 16S rRNA analysis reveal the regulatory mechanisms underlying the differences in fat deposition between distinct broiler breeds
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Baicheng oil chicken (BC) is a local Chinese breed renowned for its high intramuscular fat (IMF) content and excellent flavor. OBJECTIVES: This study compared BC with yellow-feathered broilers (YF) to investigate the mechanisms underlying significant differences in fat deposition. METHODS: Eight YF and eight BC samples were selected from 80 YF and 80 BC individuals of similar body weight, respectively, followed by transcriptomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing accordingly. RESULTS: The results showed that compared to YF, BC of the same weight had significantly less abdominal and hepatic fat deposition but a markedly higher breast muscle IMF level. Serum TG and LDL-C levels were significantly higher in the YF group than in the BC group, whereas HDL-C levels were notable lower. 16S rRNA analysis revealed an enrichment of f_Streptococcaceae and g_Lactobacillus in the YF and BC groups, respectively. Analysis of differentially expressed genes found in both liver and ileum tissues indicated enrichment primarily in the hepatic PPARG/FABP1 and intestinal PPARA/FABP1 pathways, which also influence the gut microbiota. The BC group exhibited significantly higher expression of genes related to fatty acid uptake, synthesis, and storage in breast muscle tissue (CD36 and FABP3, ACACA and FASN, and TMEM68, DGAT2, and PLIN2), while gene expression related to fatty acid oxidation was significantly lower (CPT1A and PPARA) compared to the YF group. Concurrently, the expression of lipoprotein receptors (LDLR and SCARB1) was significantly higher in the BC group than in the YF group. Spearman correlation analysis showed that the gut microbiota was influenced by the hepatic PPARG/FABP1 and intestinal PPARA/FABP1 pathways, confirming that the gut-liver axis jointly contributed to the distinct fat deposition patterns observed in the two broiler chicken breeds. CONCLUSIONS: These findings have significant implications for improving chicken meat quality.

title: Methadone induces phospholipidosis and lysosomal dysfunction in astrocytes in vitro and in the developing brain
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Methadone maintenance therapy is the standard treatment for opioid dependence during pregnancy, as its long half-life helps prevent relapse to short-acting abused opioids. However, the cellular mechanisms underlying methadone's neurodevelopmental toxicity remain poorly understood. Lipid dysregulation has emerged as a pathological feature in several neurological conditions and may contribute to cognitive impairment in children exposed to methadone in utero. OBJECTIVES: To determine whether methadone exposure alters lipid homeostasis in astrocytes and to assess whether such alterations are associated with cellular dysfunction and inflammatory responses. METHODS: Primary rat astrocytes were treated with methadone for three days. Lipid accumulation, lipid droplet formation, and lysosomal distribution were assessed using BODIPY-493/503, perilipin-2 immunostaining, and LysoTracker, respectively, followed by confocal microscopy and colocalization analyses. Ultrastructural changes were examined by electron microscopy. Lipid composition was quantified by mass spectrometry-based lipidomics. Findings were validated in cortical organotypic cultures and in the cortex of pups born to methadone-exposed dams using RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence, and ultrastructural analyses. Translational relevance was further assessed in primary human fetal astrocytes. RESULTS: Methadone exposure induced a dose and time-dependent accumulation of lysosomal lipids in primary neonatal rat astrocytes, independent of lipid droplet formation and opioid receptor activation. Electron microscopy revealed multilamellar bodies characteristic of drug-induced phospholipidosis, a known effect of many cationic amphiphilic drugs. Lipidomics confirmed elevated levels of ceramides and triglycerides. Methadone-treated astrocytes displayed impaired lysosomal degradation capacity, indicating functional compromise. Similar lysosomal and inflammatory alterations were observed in methadone-exposed organotypic cultures and in the cortex of offspring from methadone-treated dams. Human fetal astrocytes replicated these findings, demonstrating cross-species conservation. CONCLUSION: Methadone induces phospholipidosis and lysosomal dysfunction in astrocytes, accompanied by neuroinflammatory activation during brain development. These findings uncover an unrecognized mechanism linking methadone's amphiphilic properties to developmental neurotoxicity and emphasize the need to re-evaluate the safety of methadone use during pregnancy.

title: Biotransformation and applications of selenium nanoparticles for sustainable agriculture
abstract: BACKGROUND: Selenium (Se) is an essential trace element for human and plant health, yet its deficiency affects nearly one billion people globally due to low soil availability and inefficient dietary supplementation. Conventional inorganic and organic Se forms face significant challenges, including low bioavailability, potential toxicity, and poor assimilation by plants. Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) have emerged as a promising nano-formulation that combines the advantages of both inorganic and organic forms while mitigating their drawbacks, offering higher bioavailability, controlled release, and reduced toxicity. AIM OF REVIEW: This review examines the biotransformation and multifaceted applications of SeNPs in agricultural systems, with an emphasis on their synthesis, mechanisms of action, and efficacy in enhancing crop productivity, metabolite profile, nutritional quality, and stress resilience. Furthermore, we highlight the new and promising avenues of SeNPs and their application potential in modern agriculture. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS OF REVIEW: This review systematically examines; 1) biological synthesis routes using bacteria, fungi, microalgae, and plants with physicochemical methods, highlighting challenges in scalability and reproducibility. 2) the mechanism of SeNPs uptake, transport, and assimilation in plants, and their efficiency in Se biofortification. 3) the role of SeNPs in promoting plant growth, photosynthesis, phytohormone modulation, and biosynthesis of primary and secondary metabolites. 4) the efficacy of SeNPs in mitigating abiotic stresses such as heavy metal toxicity, salinity, drought, heat and biotic stresses from pathogens and pests. Finally, key bottlenecks in large-scale production, environmental fate, toxicological considerations, and future directions for the sustainable integration of SeNPs into agriculture are critically discussed.

title: The xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolase TaXTH16 enhances wheat drought tolerance and pre-harvest sprouting resistance via ABA-mediated pathways
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Drought and PHS are major constraints on wheat production worldwide. Cell wall remodeling plays a crucial role in plant adaptation to water deficit. Xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolases (XTHs) are key cell wall-modifying enzymes, yet how they integrate with ABA signaling, the central pathway controlling drought responses and seed dormancy, remains unknown in wheat. OBJECTIVES: The primary objective of this study is to functionally characterize TaXTH16 in drought tolerance and PHS resistance, with a focus on its transcriptional regulation by ABA responsive transcription factors and its natural haplotype variation for breeding applications. METHODS: We generated TaXTH16 overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout wheat lines for drought and PHS phenotyping. We performed biochemical assays for XET activity and subcellular localization, physiological measurements of water loss rate, stomatal aperture, ABA content, and ROS levels, transcriptomic analysis, and molecular assays including Y1H, EMSA, ChIP-qPCR, and dual-luciferase. Haplotype analyses were conducted across a wide range of wheat accessions. RESULTS: TaXTH16 encodes a functional XET enzyme localized to the plasma membrane and cell wall. Overexpression of TaXTH16 significantly enhanced drought tolerance, whereas knockout lines were more sensitive. TaXTH16 promoted xyloglucan and cellulose accumulation and enhanced ABA-mediated stomatal closure and ROS scavenging under drought. It also positively regulated PHS resistance, likely via ABA-mediated pathways. TaABF2 was identified as a direct transcriptional activator of TaXTH16. A natural variant, TaXTH16-2B-HapII, showed a higher promoter activity, significant association with greater drought resistance, and enrichment in modern cultivars. CONCLUSION: This study establishes TaXTH16 as a positive regulator of wheat drought tolerance and PHS resistance, linking ABA signaling and cell wall remodeling. TaXTH16 is directly activated by TaABF2, and TaXTH16-2B-HapII represents a promising allele for breeding. These findings provide mechanistic insights into ABA-cell wall crosstalk and a valuable resource for improving wheat stress resilience.

title: A three-hit sequential model of chemo-brain: from peripheral inflammation to central oxidative stress and synaptic dysfunction
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chemotherapy-induced central neurotoxicity (CICN), commonly known as "chemo-brain", is a prevalent and debilitating condition in cancer survivors, characterized by persistent cognitive deficits that severely compromise quality of life. Despite extensive research, the pathophysiology of CICN remains fragmented, lacking a unifying model that explains how it progresses from peripheral insult to chronic cognitive consolidation. AIM OF REVIEW: This review proposes a novel Three-Hit sequential model to reconceptualize CICN as a dynamic, staged pathological continuum. Unlike existing multi-hit hypotheses that largely describe cumulative or concurrent CNS risk factors, the Three-Hit model features a therapy-triggered, outside-in cascade with defined temporal checkpoints. The model aims to unify disparate mechanistic findings, explain the enduring nature of cognitive deficits after treatment cessation, and guide stage-specific, mechanism-based precision interventions. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS OF REVIEW: The model delineates three sequential pathological phases. The First Hit (peripheral priming) involves chemotherapy-induced gut dysbiosis and systemic inflammation. The Second Hit (central amplification) entails blood-brain barrier disruption, microglial activation, and oxidative stress-driven synaptic dysfunction. The Third Hit (network consolidation) is defined by epigenetic reprogramming, cellular senescence, and white matter degradation, which collectively solidify chronic cognitive impairment. This staged model may facilitate the design of phase-targeted interventions, including microbiota modulation (First Hit), anti-inflammatory and BBB-stabilizing agents (Second Hit), and senotherapeutics or HDAC6 inhibitors (Third Hit), and may guide neuroprotective strategies toward better-timed application. By linking mechanistic insights to a staged biomarker ecosystem, this review offers a conceptual roadmap for advancing stage-specific therapies for CICN.

title: Identifying phase separation modulators mediated by the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein using a structure-based drug discovery approach
abstract: INTRODUCTION: As severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to evolve through mutations and acquire resistance to existing antiviral agents, the persistence of post-pandemic infections remains a significant global health concern. To address these challenges, it is crucial to develop novel therapeutic agents that target previously unexplored viral or host mechanisms. OBJECTIVES: The nucleocapsid (N) protein of SARS-CoV-2 plays a critical role in viral RNA replication and genome packaging through its ability to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Targeting the condensation of N-RNA complex could potentially serve as an effective therapeutic strategy against coronavirus infections. The present study provides a successful exemplification of antiviral agent discovery by targeting the viral N protein on the basis of its structural characteristics. METHODS: A total of 23 virtual screening compounds and 16 hit derivatives were prepared. Their binding affinity and antiviral activities were evaluated using surface plasmon resonance and immunofluorescence assay, respectively. The impact of these compounds on condensate formation was verified through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, as well as the inhibition of N condensate formation in cells. RESULTS: Structure-based virtual screening, target protein binding affinity quantification, and cell culture-based anti-SARS-CoV-2 assays enabled the identification a hit compound, D21. Subsequent structural optimization of series I and II yielded compound II8, which exhibits stronger binding affinity for the N protein and effectively inhibits the formation of N-RNA condensates, thereby demonstrating its potential to modulate LLPS, a mechanism underlying its antiviral activity. In vivo evaluation showed that II8 displays antiviral activity in a human ACE2-expressing mouse model when administered intranasally as a pre-incubated mixture with SARS-CoV-2. Due to the pharmacokinetic profile of compound II8, further structural modifications are still required. CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that compound II8 may serve as a localized prophylactic nasal spray, providing valuable insights for further development of LLPS modulators as next-generation antiviral agents.

title: Cellular metabolic reprogramming in periodontitis: advanced therapeutic strategies and periodontal regeneration
abstract: BACKGROUND: Periodontitis is one of the most prevalent chronic inflammatory diseases worldwide, ultimately leading to tooth loss and masticatory dysfunction. Effective treatment of periodontitis requires not only control of inflammation but also regeneration of various cell types and tissues. Recent studies have shown that metabolic reprogramming in the periodontal microenvironment serves as a key link between inflammatory responses and an imbalance in bone homeostasis. Metabolic reprogramming not only drives disease progression but also profoundly influences tissue repair. AIM: of review: This article provides a comprehensive review of metabolic reprogramming in immune cells and bone-related cells during periodontitis, with a particular focus on how metabolic abnormalities impair the osteogenic differentiation capacity of periodontal ligament stem cells and disrupt the balance between osteogenesis and osteolysis. Additionally, we highlight therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic pathways, especially those based on biomaterials, which can modulate the metabolism of immune cells and bone cells for periodontal regeneration. Finally, this review discusses future directions and emerging technologies in this field, aiming to offer theoretical support and clinical reference for a deeper understanding ofthe intricate interactive network of cell metabolism, immune response and bone remodeling and to develop precise strategies for periodontitis. Key scientific concepts of review: During periodontitis, distinct cell populations exhibit unique metabolic phenotypes: immune cells sustain inflammation via glycolysis, while bone-resident cells undergo metabolic shifts that impair their regenerative capacity. Restoring metabolic balance suppresses aberrant immunity, enhances bone formation, and creates a favorable microenvironment for periodontal regeneration. This review highlights emerging therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic pathways, particularly metabolism-modulating biomaterials. By integrating current advances, this review aims to elucidate the links among metabolism, immunity, and bone homeostasis, offering new directions for precise regenerative therapies in periodontitis.

title: The stimulative effect of Cordyceps sinensis functionalized selenium nanoparticles on bone development in growing mice: involvement of the gut microbiota-bone axis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Achieving optimal peak bone mass (PBM) during adolescence through adequate intake of trace element such as selenium is crucial for reducing osteoporosis risk in later life. We previously developed novel functionalized selenium nanoparticles (Cs4-SeNPs) utilizing polysaccharide-protein complex isolated from Cordyceps sinensis for prevention of osteoporosis. The gut microbiota, functioning as the "second gene pool", plays a crucial role in maintaining bone homeostasis. However, how Cs4-SeNPs regulate bone metabolism via the gut microbiota-bone axis remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: To elucidate how the gut microbiota and microbial metabolites mediate the bone-promoting effect of Cs4-SeNPs. METHODS: Growing mice model was used to assess the effect of Cs4-SeNPs on bone development. Metagenomics, metabolomics, and proteomics analyses were conducted to uncover the mechanism of action of Cs4-SeNPs. In vitro osteoblast and osteoclast models were employed to validate the effects of key gut microbial metabolites regulated by Cs4-SeNPs on osteogenesis and osteoclastogenesis. Pseudo-germ-free mice model treated with antibiotics was employed to determine the role of gut microbiota in bone-promoting effects of Cs4-SeNPs. RESULTS: We found that Cs4-SeNPs significantly enhanced bone mass in growing mice, as evidenced by improved bone microarchitecture and increased expression of bone extracellular matrix-related markers. Notably, antibiotic treatment-induced microbial depletion abolished the effects of Cs4-SeNPs on bone development in growing mice. Increased abundance of beneficial gut bacterial genera, notably Adlercreutzia and Parvibacter, were observed following Cs4-SeNPs administration. Proteomics analysis and subsequent verification experiments demonstrated that Cs4-SeNPs inhibited the TNF-R1/TAB2/NF-κB inflammatory pathway and upregulated the expression of antioxidant proteins including SERPINA3K, GPX1, and SOD in the bone tissue. Metabolomic analysis revealed that Cs4-SeNPs treatment significantly elevated fecal and serum levels of two key metabolites: kynurenic acid and trehalose. Further in vitro studies confirmed that kynurenic acid and trehalose could reproduce the effects of Cs4-SeNPs on osteoblastic and osteoclastic differentiation. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that Cs4-SeNPs optimize PBM and promote bone development in growing mice by improving the osteoblast/osteoclast balance via the modulation of the inflammatory TNF-R1/TAB2/NF-κB axis and the enhancement of antioxidant activity through the elevated levels of gut microbial metabolites kynurenic acid and trehalose in a gut microbiota-dependent manner.

title: Uqcrc2 lactylation promotes sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy by targeting the mitochondrial respiratory chain
abstract: BACKGROUND: Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SIC) markedly increases the overall mortality among patients with sepsis. The pathogenesis of SIC remains incompletely elucidated; specifically, the role of protein lactylation in the onset and progression of SIC awaits further investigation. METHODS: Using lactylome profilinganalysis, bioinformatics and molecular biology methods, the key proteins and lactylation sites involved in the development of SIC were identified. Amino acid point mutations, molecular dynamic simulation, and biochemical experiments were performed to investigate their biological roles and underlying mechanisms. RESULTS: The lactylome analysis revealed 439 differentially lactylated sites in the myocardium of septic mice compared with control group.Through integrated bioinformatic analysis and molecular validation, we demonstrated that lactylation of ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase core protein 2 (Uqcrc2) plays a pivotal role in SIC, andidentified K109 as the critical lactylation site. Mechanistically,Uqcrc2 K109 lactylation disrupts mitochondrial respiratory chain function and exacerbates cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Importantly,inhibition of Uqcrc2 K109 lactylation attenuates this apoptotic process. Furthermore, we identifiedlysine acetyltransferase 6A (KAT6A) as a novel lactyltransferase, mediating Uqcrc2 lactylation. CONCLUSIONS: Our study reveals that the lactate-KAT6A-Uqcrc2 lactylation-mitochondrial apoptosis axis plays a pivotal role in SIC.

title: Ziyu glycoside I suppresses senescence and ameliorates age-related functional decline by stabilizing LDHA and restoring lactate output
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cellular senescence contributes to age-related tissue dysfunction and is closely linked to metabolic remodeling and mitochondrial redox imbalance. However, senotherapeutic strategies with defined molecular targets and functionally validated downstream mechanisms remain limited. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify natural-product modulators of cellular senescence and determine whether their anti-senescence activity is mediated through a targetable metabolic pathway. METHODS: An image-based high-content screen of 175 medicinal extracts identified candidate anti-senescence agents. The lead compound was validated across mammalian cell models, Caenorhabditis elegans, and mouse models of D-galactose (D-gal)-induced and physiological aging. Mechanistic studies combined target-engagement and protein-stability assays, genetic and pharmacological perturbations, proteomics, and metabolic and mitochondrial analyses. RESULTS: Ziyu glycoside I (Zg I), a triterpenoid saponin from Sanguisorba officinalis, suppressed senescence-associated phenotypes across multiple cellular models. In C. elegans, Zg I extended lifespan, improved locomotor and physiological fitness, reduced age-associated biomarkers, and enhanced oxidative stress resistance. In D-gal-induced and naturally aging mice, Zg I attenuated functional decline and multiorgan abnormalities. Mechanistically, Zg I directly engaged lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA), reduced LDHA-associated ubiquitination, and slowed proteasomal turnover, thereby preserving LDHA abundance and restoring lactate production. LDHA depletion or LDH inhibition weakened the anti-senescence effects of Zg I, whereas lactate supplementation rescued senescence-associated phenotypes in LDHA-depleted cells. Pharmacological and genetic perturbations further implicated lactylation-associated regulation downstream of the LDHA-lactate axis. Proteomic and functional analyses revealed coordinated remodeling of glucose metabolism and improved mitochondrial redox and bioenergetic homeostasis. In naturally aged mice, inhibition of lactate production attenuated Zg I-mediated suppression of tissue senescence and injury despite preserved LDHA restoration. CONCLUSION: Zg I suppresses senescence and age-related dysfunction by directly engaging and stabilizing LDHA, thereby restoring lactate-dependent metabolic output. These findings identify the LDHA-lactate axis as a mechanistically defined and potentially actionable pathway for geroprotective intervention.

title: Interfacial synergism of surface oxygen and cation redox chemistry in Co3O4–Mn3O4 heterostructures for low-temperature catalytic oxidation (LTCO) of benzene: stable humid-state activity after initial water inhibition
abstract: Introduction Low-temperature catalytic oxidation (LTCO) is a promising route to mitigate hazardous aromatic volatile organic compounds (VOCs) such as benzene, yet catalyst activity and water inhibition remain significant challenges. Objectives This study aims to develop dual-phase Co 3 O 4 –Mn 3 O 4 heterostructures (CM-x; x = Co/Mn molar ratio of 0.3–3) for the LTCO of dilute benzene and to elucidate how phase distribution, surface oxygen speciation, reducibility, and water adsorption govern performance under humid conditions (RH = 0–100%). Methods CM-x heterostructures were synthesized by coprecipitation and evaluated in a fixed-bed reactor for the oxidation of 10 ppm benzene at 50–550 °C under varying relative humidity (RH = 0–100%). Results Under dry-feed conditions, CM-1 exhibits the highest benzene oxidation activity, with T 50 = 227 °C and T 90 = 317 °C, and the most favorable balance between deep oxidative mineralization and CO 2 formation. At 250 °C, its mass-normalized benzene oxidation rate (5.06 × 10 −5 mol·gcat −1 ·h −1 ) exceeds those of CM-3, CM-0.3, Co 3 O 4 , and Mn 3 O 4 by factors of 1.1, 1.6, 7.8, and 20.3, respectively. Although the steady-state activity of CM-1 declines by ≈ 49% at 50% RH relative to the dry phase, a stable activity plateau is reached as humidity increases from 50 to 100% RH. These trends are consistent with redox synergy between Co 3+ /Co 2+ and Mn 4+ /Mn 3+ /Mn 2+ , coupled with changes in lattice and surface oxygen species, which together promote benzene activation and the subsequent deep oxidative mineralization of oxygenated intermediates to CO 2 . Conclusion The Co/Mn ratio in Co 3 O 4 –Mn 3 O 4 heterostructures thus governs benzene oxidation through coupled changes in phase distribution, surface oxygen speciation, reducibility, and water adsorption, underscoring the potential of these dual-phase oxides for the low-temperature thermocatalytic abatement of aromatic VOCs.

title: Rapid and label-free analysis of biological characteristics of hepatocelluar carcinoma tissues based on histological images
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity, complicating treatment selection and clinical management. OBJECTIVES: We developed an artificial intelligence-based histopathological framework to predict HCC biological characteristics from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides. METHODS: Using The Cancer Genome Atlas Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (TCGA-LIHC) cohort, transcriptomic phenotypes associated with angiogenesis, stemness, and autophagy were identified through gene set analysis, differential expression analysis, and consensus clustering, and evaluated for overall survival and drug sensitivity. Whole-slide images were processed into 224 × 224-pixel tumor tiles for phenotype prediction using feature extraction (UNI, ResNet50, CTrans, GigaPath, and Virchow2) combined with classic multiple instance learning and clustering-constrained attention-based multiple instance learning.. Models were externally validated at Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University and Tongji Hospital. Interpretability was assessed using attention heatmaps, and predictions were evaluated against molecular markers and tumor differentiation grades. RESULTS: Unsupervised clustering identified two subgroups per phenotype, with significant difference in survival (all p < 0.004) and sensitivities to sorafenib or transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (all p < 0.0001). The tumor detection model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 97.53%. The phenotype prediction models achieved internal optimal AUCs of 85.51%-91.05% and accuracies of 79.63%-88.89%. External optimal AUCs were 70.94%, 88.64%, and 91.17% for angiogenesis, stemness, and autophagy, with accuracies of 62.00%, 78.00%, and 84.00%, respectively. Attention heatmaps revealed distinct morphological features among subgroups, including neovascularization, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, and cytoplasmic vacuolization. Model predictions showed concordance with CD31/CD105 (κ = 0.398-0.432), CD133/LGR5 (κ = 0.428-0.629), Beclin-1/p62-LC3B (κ = 0.592-0.762) (all p < 0.05), and tumor differentiation grade (κ = - 0.167 to - 0.175, p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: This proof-of-concept AI framework predicted transcriptome-defined HCC phenotypes from routine histology, with predictions associated with prognosis and therapeutic response. It may provide a cost-effective approach for assessing HCC heterogeneity and complement molecular profiling.

title: Restoring the repair–fibrosis balance via a localized extracellular vesicle–pirfenidone dual-delivery biomaterial platform promotes ureteral repair after thermal injury
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Ureteral thermal injury can lead to ureteral stricture through persistent oxidative stress, inflammation, impaired vascular repair, and excessive fibrosis. Current treatment strategies primarily aim to restore urinary drainage or address established structural obstruction, whereas approaches that simultaneously modulate tissue repair and postinjury fibrotic remodeling remain limited. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to develop a localized dual-delivery biomaterial platform that simultaneously promotes tissue repair and suppresses excessive fibrosis after ureteral thermal injury. METHODS: A localized EG_PFM platform was fabricated by combining a mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle (MSC-EV)-loaded chitosan/hyaluronic acid hydrogel (EG) with a pirfenidone (PF)-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanofibrous membrane (PFM). The physicochemical properties and release profiles were characterized. In vitro, the effects of MSC-EVs and PF on urothelial and smooth muscle cell relative cell growth and migration, oxidative stress, angiogenesis, macrophage phenotype, and fibrosis-associated cellular responses were evaluated. A rabbit model of ureteral thermal injury was established to assess ureteral structural repair, hydronephrosis, collagen deposition, oxidative stress, inflammation, angiogenesis, and transcriptomic changes. RESULTS: EG_PFM exhibited favorable biocompatibility, tissue adhesion, and sustained release of MSC-EVs and PF. MSC-EVs increased relative cell growth and enhanced the migration of urothelial and smooth muscle cells, reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species, enhanced endothelial tube formation and were associated with an M2-like macrophage phenotype, whereas PF suppressed α-SMA expression and extracellular matrix accumulation. In rabbits, EG_PFM reduced hydronephrosis and ureteral stricture, decreased collagen deposition, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses, and enhanced vascularization. Transcriptomic analysis identified treatment-associated changes in multiple signaling and metabolic pathways, including calcium signaling, cell adhesion molecules, tyrosine metabolism, and retinol metabolism. CONCLUSION: Localized codelivery of MSC-EVs and PF promoted reparative responses while limiting fibrotic remodeling, thereby improving structural repair after ureteral thermal injury. EG_PFM represents a promising localized therapeutic strategy for reducing postinjury ureteral stricture.

title: Yeast protein-derived methionine alleviates ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury by targeting TNF-α/NOS2 and modulating the NOD-like receptor signaling pathway
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Ethanol directly stimulates and damages the gastric mucosa, leading to impairment of the mucus-bicarbonate barrier and mechanical barrier, which is the primary factor of gastric ulcer formation. Yeast protein (YP), an emerging microbial food ingredient, has shown potential in mucosal protection. However, its bioactive components and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the protective effect of YP hydrolyzed by papanin (YP-P) against ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury, identify the key bioactive compound, and elucidate the molecular mechanism by which it alleviates gastric mucosal damage. METHODS: In this study, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence (IF), western blotting (WB), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and other experimental techniques were used to evaluate the protective effects of YP-P by establishing ethanol-induced gastric mucosal injury models in vitro and in vivo. RNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, peptidomics, virtual screening, molecular docking, network pharmacology, proteomics, and multi-omics analysis techniques were used to determine the potential targets and molecular mechanisms of YP-P in alleviating gastric mucosal damage. Finally, the inhibition of bioactive compounds identified in YP on the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor signaling pathway was verified through cell experiments. RESULTS: The protective effects of papain-hydrolyzed YP (YP-P) were demonstrated by establishing ethanol-induced gastric mucosal injury models in vitro and in vivo. Fractionation via centrifugation and ultrafiltration identified the component with molecular weight less than 5 kDa (YP-P < 5 kDa) as the primary protective fraction. Integrating multi-omics with virtual screening and network pharmacology, methionine (Met) was identified as the key bioactive compound within YP-P < 5 kDa. Mechanism studies revealed that Met alleviates ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury by targeting tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)/inducible nitrogen oxide synthase (NOS2) and modulating the NOD-like receptor signaling pathway. CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight the protective effect of YP and its bioactive compound in the prevention and management of gastric mucosal injury, providing reference for their application as gastric mucosal protectants in functional ingredient.

title: Canagliflozin ameliorates ferroptosis in diabetic podocytes by PCBP1-enriched extracellular vesicles derived from proximal tubular epithelial cells
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Podocyte ferroptosis contributes to proteinuria in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Canagliflozin reduces albuminuria, but the mechanism underlying podocyte protection remains unclear. Because sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) is expressed predominantly in proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTECs) rather than podocytes, we hypothesized that this effect is mediated indirectly through PTEC-derived signals. OBJECTIVES: To determine whether canagliflozin suppresses podocyte ferroptosis through PTEC-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) and to define the underlying molecular mechanism. METHODS: A matched subset of 60 patients with DKD (CON, n = 30; CANA, n = 30) from a prospective, multicenter, randomized, open-label trial was analyzed to assess clinical associations. Mechanistic studies were performed in cultured PTECs and podocytes, db/db mice, and renal tubule-specific Foxo1-knockout mice. EV dependence was examined using GW4869. EV proteomics, luciferase reporter assays, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and RNA immunoprecipitation were used to delineate the FOXO1/VPS53-PCBP1/ACSL4 pathway. iRGD-modified PCBP1-enriched EVs were further evaluated in db/db mice. RESULTS: In cultured podocytes, canagliflozin did not directly alter ferroptosis-related changes, whereas EVs from canagliflozin-treated PTECs were protective. In PTECs, canagliflozin promoted FOXO1 nuclear translocation and VPS53 transcription, thereby increasing EV release. The improvement in renal injury and ferroptosis-related markers was attenuated in diabetic mice with renal tubule-specific Foxo1 deletion. EVs derived from canagliflozin-treated PTECs were enriched in PCBP1, which bound ACSL4 mRNA and reduced its stability in podocytes, thereby limiting lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. iRGD-modified PCBP1-enriched EVs ameliorated renal injury and reduced ferroptosis-related changes in db/db mice. CONCLUSION: The experimental findings support a FOXO1/VPS53-dependent PTEC-EV pathway associated with PCBP1-mediated destabilization of ACSL4 mRNA and protection against ferroptosis in cultured podocytes. These findings identify tubule-to-podocyte EV communication as a mechanism underlying canagliflozin-mediated podocyte protection and support further evaluation of PCBP1-enriched EVs as a potential EV-based therapeutic strategy for DKD.

title: Associations of gut microbial and serum metabolic features with metabolic comorbidities in patients with NAFLD
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) coexists with dyslipidemia or impaired fasting glucose (IFG), but gut microbial and serum metabolic features remain incompletely characterized. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to compare gut microbial beta diversity, taxonomic profiles, predicted microbial functions, and serum metabolites across healthy controls (HCs) and NAFLD subgroups; evaluate omics-based classifiers and exploratory integrated classifiers distinguishing subgroups from HCs; and assess metabolic responses to Dialister invisus supplementation in mice. METHODS: Fecal microbiota and serum metabolites were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted UPLC-MS/MS, respectively, in 41 HCs and 222 NAFLD patients. Patients were stratified into three subgroups by dyslipidemia and IFG: NAFLD_N (neither dyslipidemia nor IFG), NAFLD_DLP (dyslipidemia without IFG), and NAFLD_IFG (IFG irrespective of lipid status; HbA1c/OGTT unavailable). Random-forest classifiers were developed for each omics layer and for post hoc integrated multi-omics panels to distinguish each NAFLD subgroup from HCs, with performance evaluated in the held-out set. Dialister invisus was administered to high-calorie diet-fed mice, and metabolic and hepatic outcomes were assessed. RESULTS: NAFLD patients showed lower Dialister invisus abundance and higher abundance of the GTDB placeholder taxon Phascolarctobacterium_A sp900545025, with increased predicted menaquinone biosynthetic potential. Microbial and serum metabolite profiles differed significantly among subgroups. Microbiome classifiers achieved AUROCs of 0.71, 0.58, and 0.73 in the held-out internal evaluation, whereas metabolome classifiers achieved AUROCs of 0.89, 0.83, and 0.93 for NAFLD_N, NAFLD_DLP, and NAFLD_IFG. Post hoc integrated panels yielded descriptive AUROCs of 0.92, 0.89, and 0.96 in that subset. Dialister invisus supplementation reduced body weight, serum ALT, AST, triglycerides, fasting blood glucose, and ipGTT AUC in high-calorie diet-fed mice. CONCLUSION: This study identifies shared gut microbial and serum metabolic alterations across NAFLD patients irrespective of IFG or dyslipidemia, alongside subgroup-specific signatures. The Dialister invisus findings support its potential role in metabolic regulation and warrant mechanistic investigation.

title: An integrative GWAS, Transcriptomic, and domestication analysis Uncovers Multi-Layered genetic architecture of kernel rate in maize testcross hybrids
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Improving yield efficiency in maize (Zea mays L.) is increasingly important under high-density production systems, where gains from total biomass accumulation are approaching physiological limits. Kernel Rate (KR), or shelling percentage, captures reproductive biomass partitioning within the ear but remains less well characterized genetically than absolute yield components. OBJECTIVE: Here, we evaluated KR together with ear weight (EW), cob weight (CW), and kernel weight (KW) in two testcross populations generated with Mo17 and Zheng58 and assessed across six year-by-location environments. KR was highly heritable, showed only weak correlations with EW, and was consistently negatively correlated with CW, supporting its use as an index of relative kernel-to-cob biomass allocation. METHODS: testcross performance, and population genomic signals from domestication scans. Rather than identifying a single set of causal genes, this approach revealed limited overlap among data layers, indicating that yield efficiency is shaped by multiple, context-dependent genetic contributions. RESULTS: GWAS identified multiple trait-associated loci with limited overlap across environments and tester backgrounds; two CW associations also met FDR_BH < 0.05. Parental-line PCA showed partial but incomplete differentiation between high- and low-performance groups. PERMANOVA attributed 18.8-23.4 % of transcriptomic variation to group membership, with significant differences for CW and KW and weaker evidence for EW and KR. Integration of association, expression, and evolutionary evidence prioritized representative candidates including FDPS3, PFK/FBPase, and Zm00001d038275. CONCLUSION: These results support a multi-layered and context-dependent genetic basis of biomass partitioning in maize testcross hybrids. The integrative framework provides biologically informed candidate priorities for functional validation and breeding across additional testers and environments.

title: Targeting lactate-GPR81/TAZ/PPARα-induced ROS in Bregs overcomes immunosuppression and improves lung cancer outcomes
abstract: Introduction Tumor-derived lactic acid (LA) plays a dual role in shaping the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by directly modulating immune cell function. Objectives Tumor-infiltrating B cells enhance antitumor immunity by promoting T-cell proliferation, whereas immunosuppressive subsets such as regulatory B cells (Bregs) counteract these effects via IL-10 sretion. However, the metabolic impact of lactate on B-cell functionality remains unclear. Methods Using flow cytometry, we analyzed LA-induced phenotypic alterations in B cells and assessed Breg immunosuppressive activity via suppression assays. The tumor-inhibitory effects of blocking lactate receptor signaling were examined in animal models. Results Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized immunosuppressive mechanism mediated by CD25 + CD81 + B cells (Bregs) in lung cancer. In murine models, LA induced ROS production in splenic and intratumoral Bregs through G protein-coupled receptor 81 (GPR81) signaling, thereby suppressing T-cell responses. Mechanistically, LA binding to GPR81 activates the cAMP/TAZ/PPARα axis, which orchestrates ROS generation in Bregs. Genetic ablation of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) in tumor cells disrupted this signaling cascade in vivo , resulting in reduced ROS levels and restored T-cell activity. Pharmacological inhibition of GPR81 or PPARα similarly attenuated Breg-mediated immunosuppression and delayed tumor progression. Clinically, we identified ROS + Breg populations in lung cancer patients, and elevated tumor LDHA expression correlated with poor prognosis. Conclusion Our findings establish the LA-GPR81/TAZ/PPARα/ROS axis in Bregs as a redox-dependent checkpoint for tumor immune evasion, and highlighting novel therapeutic targets for lung cancer immunotherapy.
